author: Feven Merid
title: Where the mouse eats the cat
content:
“Welcome to the Central Prison of Douala,” La PJ, an inmate and a star of the documentary

Jail Time Records

, says in an opening scene of the film. “The place where the mouse eats the cat.” Dione Roach, one of the film’s directors, offered me an interpretation: “The world is upside down in prison; the mouse can be more shrewd,” she said. The intimate glimpse into the Central Prison of Douala, also known as New Bell Prison, does indeed reveal an upside-down world. Like many prisons, its inmates recreate the contours of outside life on the inside, but in New Bell it’s taken to another level. There are actual neighborhoods like the Latin Quarter, home to the Emperor and his gang known as the Latinos, and the Base, where the prisoners who make up the quasi police squad reside. There’s a marketplace for people to sell fried foods and taxis, except these taxis are inmates who swiftly run through the congested prison to hand-deliver messages. They even have a “homeless” population, those who must sleep outside in the courtyard because there aren’t enough beds. Their neighborhood is dubbed House of the Penguins.

This all comes into focus when you learn New Bell is notoriously overcrowded — it was built for 800 people but currently holds almost 6,000. Thus, the prison has been transformed into a mini city, colloquially referred to by inmates as the 11th province of Cameroon (there are officially 10). La PJ, a lanky and charismatic man dressed in his uniform of a conductor’s hat, blazer, and tie, steps in as mayor to give us the lay of the land. “Our jewel of jewels,” he says, as he approaches his final stop on this tour — a recording studio. Specifically, it’s the Jail Time Records studio, for which the film is named and the reason for its making.

Jail Time Records, the recording studio, is the first to be put in an African prison, according to the film’s directors and the studio’s founders Dione Roach and Steve Happi. The two run it as a nonprofit music label for inmates and those who are readjusting to life outside of prison. From its start in 2018, the duo has been documenting the studio’s impact; first, inadvertently, through shooting music videos and then with the intention to make a documentary. Roach, who is from Italy and has been based in Cameroon since 2017, has served as the studio’s artistic director, and Happi, who is from Cameroon, as its lead producer (Happi was incarcerated at New Bell for two years, during which time he met Roach and helped get the studio up and running). Shot over six years, they’ve created a film that captures the curiosities of New Bell remarkably well (

Jail Time Records

 won top prizes at Tribeca Film Festival in New York). A few weeks ago, I spoke to the two directors over Zoom about what it’s like documenting New Bell, the music of their main characters, and how the film let them show a fuller picture of life in prison. This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Feven Merid

How did you start Jail Time Records and when did you realize you wanted to make a film about it?

Dione Roach

I was volunteering, doing art courses, and I came across a group of really talented musicians. They were incarcerated, and I just had the idea to do an album with them. And then I was even like, why just an album? Why don’t we actually build something that can stay and be used by many people? And so I proposed the recording studio to the prison, and they accepted, and we got it built. And then that’s when I met Steve, who was incarcerated at the time, and he was already a music producer and sound engineer. Someone introduced us, and I was finished volunteering, so I left him the keys of the studio. I came back a few months after, and they’d been doing like so much work and recording, and it had really become this like place of like extreme creativity and outlet.

Steve Happi

Before even starting the movie, I was already doing music videos and having access with the camera inside prison when I was still incarcerated. So as she said, it was just a natural process, and having access with the camera and such intimate moments of our life and our journey, we started recording everything.

Feven Merid

What was it like to film inside such a crowded place?

Dione Roach

At the start, we went with a friend who had like a gigantic camera, and he didn’t already work in prison as well, like so they didn’t know him, and so it just wasn’t really the right setup, you know, for that kind of space and …

author: Sergey Eledinov
title: Who Wins from Ukraine’s Drones in Mali?
content:
On 12 September, CNN

reported

 that around fifteen Ukrainian drone specialists are working with the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) in northern Mali. According to two Ukrainians deployed there, the group does not fight on the front line; it trains fighters and helps run operations. A Ukrainian operator told CNN that he coordinates the rebels’ operations remotely and that Ukrainians helped take Kidal earlier this year. Tuareg rebels and al-Qaeda-linked fighters attacked the town simultaneously, and Russian forces were forced to withdraw. Last week,

Jeune Afrique

 called the story an embarrassment for Washington, which is rebuilding ties with Bamako.


What follows is a balance sheet for seven actors in the war in Mali and in the Ukrainian episode: their interests, gains and losses.


Kyiv


Interest.

 The line Kyrylo Budanov set out while still head of military intelligence (HUR): strike Russia wherever it is present. Some analysts see the African operation as cheap and potentially rewarding, since it stretches Russian resources.


Gains.

 Tactical. Ukrainian operators reportedly help the FLA locate and attack Russian convoys, and by a Ukrainian operator’s own account Kidal was taken with their help. But fifteen specialists, even with perfect logistics for equipment deliveries, cannot raise the fighters’ level of training or conceptually change the character of the fighting. Kidal was taken by the FLA and JNIM.


Losses.

 Strategic. In 2024, after HUR spokesman Andriy Yusov said the rebels at Tinzaouaten had received all the information they needed, Mali and Niger cut diplomatic ties with Kyiv and, together with Burkina Faso, lodged a complaint with the UN Security Council accusing Ukraine of sponsoring terrorism. Ukraine’s foreign ministry denied involvement at the time and affirmed its unconditional respect for the sovereignty of other states. Two years later, Ukrainian specialists are working with the FLA on Malian soil. Since 2023 Ukraine has opened eight new diplomatic missions in Africa, and this story undermines their work.


There is a cost at home as well. Every such specialist in the Sahel, for an uncertain result, is one specialist fewer where Ukraine’s own fate is being decided.


Finally, there is the precedent. Ukraine’s right to self-defence is not in question. But Kyiv’s policy in Mali has crossed a line drawn not only by the norms of the international community but also by the US-Ukraine partnership. It sets a dangerous precedent for international law: folding support for international terrorism into the logic of confrontation with an adversary. If one state may do this, every state may.


Moscow


Interest.

 To hold Mali as Africa Corps’ anchor in the Sahel and to preserve Russia’s reputation as a reliable guarantor of regimes.


Losses.

 Military. Tinzaouaten in 2024, Kidal in 2026. According to ACLED data cited by RFI, more than 200 Russian fighters were killed in Mali between July 2024 and August 2026. Africa Corps has managed only tactical moves, but an operational breakthrough is impossible without more forces, and the Russian contingent in Mali has seen no serious change in numbers or quality. Time is working against Moscow. Nor is there an economic foothold: the military presence never turned into investment, and a gold refinery project near Bamako has gone unfinanced for more than a year. There is a reputational account too: a UN human rights report found that Malian troops and ‘foreign military personnel’ killed more than 500 people in Moura in March 2022. Yet the situation has not changed fundamentally either. Africa Corps remains, in effect, the only external force and the only means of propping up Assimi Goïta’s regime.


Gains.

 Narrative, and considerable. Russian setbacks in Mali now come with a ready explanation: the Ukrainian hand. In 2024 the Russian foreign ministry promptly seized on Mali’s break with Ukraine and presented it as the result of Kyiv’s support for terrorism. Kidal will be framed the same way. Kyiv supplies the evidence itself: Yusov’s statements, the video by Ukraine’s ambassador Yurii Pyvovarov, whom Senegal’s foreign ministry summoned to explain himself, and now the operators’ interviews with CNN. Any attack on a convoy escorted by Africa Corps will be read as Kyiv’s involvement in supporting terrorists. According to RFI, on 28 September JNIM ambushed an Africa Corps convoy near Niono, in the Ségou region. Drones struck the vehicles first, and at least …

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Limpopo district hospital ‘filthy’, ‘broken’ and leaderless
content:
Filthy conditions, a shortage of warm water, a broken emergency communications system, and unresolved complaints from nurses are some of the adversities being faced by both patients and healthcare workers at Nkhensani hospital in Giyani, Limpopo.


The root cause


According to healthcare workers stationed at the hospital, the woes at the public facility are fuelled by a lack of leadership. For the past eight years, the hospital has not had a permanent CEO. Five individuals have, in ten years, acted as CEOs on a temporary basis but were never permanently appointed.


The Limpopo department of health has blamed a lack of suitable candidates as the main reason for not appointing a permanent CEO. The CEO position has been vacant since 2016 following the removal of Themba Mhlanga.


“We are leaderless at this hospital and everyone does what they want; hence everything is a mess at Nkhensani. I can confidently tell that at night, patients at this hospital bath using cold water as warm water gets finished in the early hours of the morning; and the kitchen does not operate during the night and those who want tea or coffee are always left wanting,” said a staff nurse stationed at Nkhensani hospital.


Lives of patients at risk


The nurse further said that the hospital is filthy and rarely cleaned: “This hospital is never cleaned, we often go for days without it being cleaned and no one cares and cleaners are also never reprimanded as there is no one to reprimand them and they do as they like. This puts the lives of patients and healthcare workers at risk.”


The emergency communications system has not been working for months at the hospital and nurses are forced to use their personal cell phones during emergencies. “Alerting doctors of emergencies at this hospital has become extra difficult as we have to use our own personal cell phones because the hospital does not have a working emergency dial; it has not been working for months. What if I do not have airtime and a patient is in need of a doctor urgently? It might lead to an avoidable death of a patient,” she said.


The nurse also told

Elitsha

 that she has personally raised most of these issues with previous acting CEOs but nothing has ever been done to address her concerns. “Even if you complain to those superior to you, nothing is ever done to address your concerns. No one is prepared to take responsibility and all this has got to do with the lack of leadership at Nkhensani hospital,” she said.


Derrick Mashaba, a local community member in Giyani residing about 2 kilometres away from Nkhensani, told

Elitsha

 that he has witnessed the tumble of the hospital over the past decade. “We have witnessed the fall of our precious hospital over the past ten years. We have seen overcrowding, dilapidating buildings, shortage of water and lack of leadership, and all this has contributed to the fall of the mighty hospital,” said Mashaba.


It hurts him to see the fall of the hospital which is so close to his home. “This is a district hospital and it is supposed to be the best in our region but it is not being prioritised. A hospital as big as this one cannot operate without a permanent CEO; it is wrong and it is something which is supposed to be addressed immediately,” he said.


Limpopo health spokesperson, Neil Shikwambana said that the department is working towards appointing a permanent CEO. “The recruitment process is underway and an acting CEO has been appointed to ensure continuity during this process,” he said.

author: Njeri Wangarĩ
title: The Fallacy that is the CBE Arts Pathway
content:
“So CBC is designed for short-term training of workers. In Europe, it is used among refugee and immigrant communities who need to be integrated into the community as fast as possible with skills they can use to earn a living. In other words, the adults are assumed to have basic human abilities of cultural identity, values, communication, and social skills, and all CBC is doing is giving workers tools for the workplace.” ~

Dr Wandia Njoya 


When Hannah*, our firstborn daughter, sat for her KJSEA exams last year, she was among the thousands of pioneers transitioning to Grade 10 in the newly established Kenyan Education Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC), since rebranded to Competency-Based Education (CBE).


Like many parents, I was drunk on the PR and the political rhetoric

strungi

 that extolled the new curriculum above the 8-4-4 system, which we – a millennial generation still grappling with the side effects of exams, cramming, the Big 4 career options – blamed for our miserable lives stuck in jobs we hate but can’t quit. Not in this Kasongo economy.


We, the products of a system we felt seemed hell-bent on judging a fish based on its ability to climb a tree, together with the Ministry of Education, wanted to do away with exams completely. We had also swallowed the “talent carrot” that was dangled in front of us, whose hook – careers beyond being a doctor, lawyer, pilot, aeronautical engineer – was but a mirage for a majority of the learning population attending public schools.


Grade 10s and the indigestion of the CBE strungi


For nine years, the strong

strungi

 was given to us like prescribed medication three times a year. Take two tablets of expectations: “Below”, “Approaching”, “Meeting”, and “Exceeding Expectations”; two tablets of practical-based learning (I see you all who also spent nights making

wandindis

, printing portfolio photos, late evenings hunting for “locally available materials” and accompanying your young ones to the market for evidence photos of activities). 


This CBE has had us doing all manner of acrobatic exercises, which I found increasingly impractical. CBE has turned us all – parents and our children into local DIY scavengers. For any learner living in an urban area, some project activities border on the absurd. Take, for instance, the assignment that our son was given to make a

wandidi

 or

orutu

 (traditional musical instrument) using tin cans. And don’t even get me started on what the children in the rural areas are subjected to. How do you learn swimming lessons in fields or atop tables? 


We were sold a pipe dream for nine years, only to wake up to a nightmare early this year.


Hannah did exceptionally well and earned herself a place at a girls’ national school in Kiambu. But she was adamant about the pathway she wanted to take: Arts & Sports Science – a subject combination of fine arts, literature, French, music, and dance. This came as no surprise to us. We had spotted her affinity for the arts from as early as five years old when she began drawing characters from her favourite cartoon shows.


While Hannah had not been accepted at any of the schools of her choice, we, in our naive faith in the system, had believed that the national public school assigned to us by the ministry would indeed offer both the chosen subject combination and a conducive environment for her. 


An educator and a fierce critic of CBC, Dr Wandia Njoya had warned us for years. In

a 2019 article

, she said,


“Pathways mean that the arts will always be treated as an appendage, as something for children who do not perform well in academics or science. And those children will invariably be those attending poorly equipped schools. And that attitude towards the arts implies ALL KNOWLEDGE, not just the arts. It means we remain mediocre, uncreative, and unimaginative. It means that Kenyans will remain blocked from inventing, innovating, and creating, even as institutions perform innovation by creating ‘hubs’ and ‘innovation funds’.


As a product of public high school education, I knew that this school was no private school. I anticipated that it would be devoid of the bells and whistles that Hannah had enjoyed. Similarly, I had no illusions about the kind of culture and rigour Hannah would be exposed to. Her father and I wanted that for her. A public boarding school setting where discipline, individual and collective responsibility, and academic excellence, with infrastructure to support the Arts …

author: ROAPE
title: What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?
content:
John Molyneux’s classic statement of Marxist theory and practice

What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? was first published in 1984. The short book provided an incredibly sophisticated description of Marx’s method, and his relentless and insistent focus on the core agency of the working class.


Only the working class – however it is interpreted, described or labelled in social theory – can deliver a revolutionary anti-capitalist project. There cannot be, Molyneux argued, any substitute – no enlightened project of state development, or ‘socialist’ military leadership who deliver socialism on behalf of working people. Molyneux – in restating Marx’s central tenet – emphasised the role of the working class in their self-emancipation. Marx was the original prophet of the self-emancipation by working people. Without this class, and this project, there is simply no Marxism, no socialism, and no possibility of international revolution.


For an African audience the book speaks to multiple failed projects of socialism delivered by military coups, ‘enlightened’ governments and guerrilla movements. Each of these movements at different times dressed themselves in the language of Marxism, class and anti-imperialism but systematically broke genuine efforts at working class power.


What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? speaks directly to those on the continent trying to find a way to a genuine and emancipatory theory and practice of liberation.


Molyneux’ brilliant short book has now been reissued by the UK based publisher Bookmarks, and the Ugandan publisher Editor House Facility (EHF) who focus on readers across the African continent.


The new issue of the book comes with a major new introduction by the Ghanian socialist Gyekye Tanoh. Tanoh writes about the development and transformation of the working class on the continent since Molyneux wrote the book, and the continued capacity of this class to bring about socialist and revolutionary transformation across Africa.  


Join us for the launch of the African edition of

What is the Real Marxist Tradition?

 on 22 October at 18.30 (BST) with Gyekye Tanoh, Tafadzwa Choto

, 

Martin Empson and Mark Thomas. Reserve your place 

here

.


For readers based in Africa, John Molyneux’s 

What is the Real Marxist Tradition?

 can be purchased through Editor House Facility


here

. 


Endorsements of the book:


‘John Molyneux cuts through a century of distortion to recover Marxism’s authentic, revolutionary essence. This classic work distinguishes between living theory and dead orthodoxy, showing that Marxism is not a relic of the past but a vital method for understanding and transforming the world. It is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand capitalism and how to change it. For young activists and students alike, it is a must-read as it offers a powerful weapon for today’s struggles.’ 


Tafadzwa Choto

, International Socialist Organisation, Zimbabwe


‘In this book, John Molyneux undertakes a principled exercise by applying Marxism as a “method of analysis” to Marxism itself. He thereby provides not just a description of what Marxism is, but a method for detecting what isn’t. His application of this exercise—in the form of an autopsy of the interests and classes represented by three self-proclaimed Marxist tendencies—provides a valuable model for defining Marxist politics and organizations in our own contexts while enabling us to avoid the “hybrid ideologies of the petty bourgeoisie.” This is crucial, for us in the Global South, where reality differs greatly from that of Europe, thereby demanding a Marxism of contextualized design, not rigid imitation. The method offered is therefore a vital tool in enabling Marxist projects capable of fulfilling its role in “guiding revolutions to victory.” Such is true whether in the Global South or in global contexts marked by increasing economic complications and the co-option of Marxism by bourgeois ideologies fighting for survival amid the clear failure of neoliberal models … One need not agree with all of Molyneux’s conclusions to find his method a timely and indispensable resource.’


Muzan Alneel

,Marxist researcher and writer from Sudan


The post

What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?

 appeared first on

ROAPE

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Faisal Ali, Hassan Alnaser, Hazem Tharwat, Kidus Lemma
title: How a war in Tigray could set off a more complex fight
content:
For much of the past year, tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and authorities in the northern Tigray region had been steadily escalating toward confrontation.


The threat for those in Tigray, as much as for those in the wider region, was that the area could tip back into the kind of war that devastated the state between 2020 and 2022, but, this time, with a supercharged regional dimension. Officials in Addis Ababa and Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, have traded increasingly hostile accusations as the peace established at Pretoria frayed, while intermittent clashes and drone strikes produced episodes of serious violence. 


From the sidelines, Eritrea, Egypt, Somalia and Sudan — a pragmatic, loosely aligned anti-Ethiopia coalition — looked on. Then, on September 20, a drone struck a truck carrying more than 41 tons of food aid for displaced people in northwestern Tigray, setting the vehicle and its cargo ablaze.


Aftermath of a drone strike on a humanitarian aid truck in northwestern Tigray, September 22. Courtesy: @JoeTseGy on X


Three days later, Tigrayan forces seized three airports across the region. Fighting then spread beyond Tigray into neighboring Afar and Amhara. The federal government accused the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) of launching an offensive, while Tigrayan authorities said their forces were responding to federal attacks involving aircraft, drones, artillery and ground troops. Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Tigray after the airports were taken, while a Tigrayan official told Mada Masr that the confrontation has now become a “full war.”


The fighting broke out only days after the TPLF joined six other armed organizations in the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Coalition for Survival. The members have pledged to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establish a transitional administration. The coalition brought the TPLF together with the Amhara Fano National Movement, whose fighters had fought alongside federal forces against Tigray during the previous war, as well as the Oromo Liberation Army and movements from Ethiopia’s Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions. 


Tigrayan and Amhara forces remain divided by unresolved claims over western and southern Tigray, making their decision to enter the same alliance one of the clearest signs of how Ethiopia’s domestic conflicts have been realigning since the end of the previous war.


An Ethiopian political source who was close to the early discussions between several of the groups tells Mada Masr that contacts had been developing for roughly a year. The source says he lost interest as some of the participants established closer relationships with Sudan and what he had initially understood as a more political process moved, in his view, toward military coordination. 


Whatever the precise role played by those external relationships in bringing the alliance together, Ethiopian officials had already begun treating contacts between domestic armed opponents and neighboring states as parts of the same security problem. 


That concern had become increasingly public by May. After Ethiopian opposition figures and Eritrean officials met in Port Sudan under the banner of Tsimdo, army chief Berhanu Jula described what was taking shape as a “combined convergence” of Ethiopia’s adversaries. 


In June, Ethiopia’s foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, predicted that an Eritrean-backed TPLF attack would come during the rainy season, while Abiy declared that, despite coordination between Sudan, Eritrea and Ethiopia’s armed groups, Ethiopia had “not an iota of fear.”


In July, Abiy described an “axe politics” in which the TPLF formed the blade, Eritrea the wooden handle and an unnamed external actor the hand wielding it. The metaphor was polemical, but it reflected a security view in which domestic armed opposition, neighboring governments and contested borderlands were increasingly being read together.


With the outbreak of fighting, which has shown no signs of abating since the end of last week, the question now is will the fighting remain confined to the Ethiopian interior or will the convergence of the last six months turn Ethiopia’s war into a new, complex regional fight to remake the Horn of Africa?


…


The significance of that convergence lies partly in the weakening of a regional hierarchy that for almost three decades gave Ethiopia greater freedom than most of its neighbors to operate across the Horn’s porous borders …

author: Rosebell Kagumire
title: Who Does “Mutual Interest” Serve in an Unequal World? On EU Development Cooperation Pivot
content:
What is mutual interest in an unequal world? That’s what I was reflecting on this week in Brussels, when I joined the “Mutual interests in practice: How should Global Europe balance development, economic and geopolitical objectives?” panel at The Future of EU Development Cooperation, hosted by the European Centre for Development Policy Management (ECDPM) and Oxfam. The discussion came at a decisive moment, as the EU negotiates its next long-term budget and the Global Europe Instrument, while the Commission prepares for consultations with civil society and local authorities from 28 September to 1 October. Regional sessions include “Sub-Saharan Africa”, while global thematic sessions cover human development, the green and digital transition, democracy and human rights, and partnerships.

The EU is pivoting development cooperation towards its own economic, security and foreign policy goals through a “mutual interest” approach. But mutual interest means little unless it confronts the unequal systems that determine whose interests count, whose risks are ignored, and whose lives are rendered negotiable.

I spoke alongside H.E. Dr Naomi A. Ngwira, Ambassador of Malawi; Martin Seychell of DG INTPA; Christophe Lam of BusinessEurope; and William Roos of the EBRD, in a discussion moderated by San Bilal of ECDPM. I drew on the Afro-feminist work of the AfIP Collective, including members such as Memory Kachambwa of FEMNET, who also made a presentation, and the work of many African feminists challenging foreign policy in a time of faltering multilateralism.

For many in Africa, the EU’s pivot offers little that is new. Europe has repackaged its approach to Africa without altering the fundamentals that produce inequality. The Global Gateway has, by the EU’s own count, mobilised over €300 billion since 2021, including an Africa–Europe package of around €150 billion, and now targets €400 billion by 2027. But mutual interest is not mutual benefit: interests may overlap while benefits, risks and decision-making power remain profoundly unequal. As San Bilal writes in a new ECDPM briefing, wrapping every project “in a cosy mutual-benefit narrative is misleading.”

Africans have long critiqued, opposed and contested donor narratives and models of development financing and aid, calling for partnerships that are accountable and mindful of historical context. The pivot towards capital investment, with the private sector presented as the new magic formula, does not account for the reforms needed in relationships that remain hegemonic, rooted in a long history of colonialism and racial capitalism. Investment language alone forgoes critical responsibilities rooted in reparatory justice for the continent’s historic underdevelopment and exploitation.

The next Global Europe Instrument won’t escape imbalances. In its recommendations to the Irish Presidency, Oxfam warns that an explicit mandate to pursue EU interests “places excessive emphasis on the EU’s priorities over partner country objectives.” Development funding could build infrastructure for extracting critical raw materials, often for European firms and export, a trend “particularly visible on the African continent.” Fragile and conflict-affected states, which offer investors little, risk falling off the EU’s radar: left to their own devices, or pushed into extractive investment models that can deepen the very conflicts they need to escape.

Decolonial Afro-feminist perspectives argue that decisions and seemingly new approaches to trade, finance, security and cooperation are made within an existing unequal global order, its structures and relations, which distribute power, risk and harm unevenly. Who defines the bargain, whose trade-offs are treated as inevitable, and who is disposable before negotiations begin? In systems built to drain value from Africa, the same deal benefits Europe while Africa bears the costs. As economist Fadhel Kaboub warns, the colonial division of labour “locks you permanently at the bottom of the global value chain.”

Too often, “mutual interest” also means the interests of ruling elites: mineral agreements whose costs fall on neighbouring communities, and migration deals that serve regime survival. Amid the war in eastern DRC in 2024, the EU signed a raw materials agreement with Rwanda, which UN experts have found to back the M23 rebels. Several EU states are now in talks with Uganda and Rwanda to host “return hubs” for people deported from Europe. This is the …

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Manitoba’s handling of moose hunting an ‘infringement’ on Treaty rights: court documents
content:
A First Nation in northern Manitoba is taking the province back to court over its handling of big game licenses, claiming it infringes on Treaty rights and prior hunting agreements.


Leadership at Pimicikamak First Nation, also known as Cross Lake, claims its members should, but do not have, priority when it comes to hunting the dwindling population of moose on its traditional territory.


This is after a judge “misapprehended” a request for judicial review on Manitoba’s handling of moose hunting in 2024, according to court documents.


And while the matter is not settled, the community is also calling upon hunters to hand their licenses back for the rest of the 2026-2027 season to give the animals a chance to recover.


Pimicikamak, located approximately 520 kilometres north of Winnipeg, sits in the boreal forest and consists of approximately 10,400 hectares of land.


It’s part of

Game-Hunting Area (GHA) 9A

, which, according to Manitoba’s most recent air survey results collected in 2025, only has an estimated tally of 599 moose over 35,608 square kilometers.


According to the

Manitoba Wildlife Federation (MWF)

, the area’s bull moose population has declined by 53 per cent over the last decade.


Chief David Monias said climate change and the increasing threat of wildfires are making the moose disappear. He said that last year, wildfires burnt approximately 168,000 hectares of forest on the Nation’s territory alone.


“The territory has suffered tremendous environmental damages,” he said. “And we have a responsibility to protect that land and wildlife … to protect that land and wildlife for our people, for future generations.”


He added that Manitoba also has a responsibility to honour the inherent Treaty right to hunt, and to the

Northern Flood Agreement

, established in 1977, which was in response to the negative impacts on several First Nations from the construction of a Hydro dam.


According to the agreement, “residents of the Reserves [were granted] first priority to all the wildlife resources within their Trapline Zones, and in the rivers and lakes which were traditionally available to and used by them as a source of food supply, income-in-kind and income.”


It also states that, unless there is an overabundance of a certain animal, non-Indigenous hunters are prohibited from hunting in the area at all.


In the case of an overabundance, the province must only give out licenses after “meaningful consultation with the appropriate representatives or body representing the interests of the residents affected.”


However, according to Monias, this is not the case and licensed hunters are still allowed to hunt moose in regional trapline zones and areas for First Nations peoples without prior consultation.


Monias pictured at the AFN gathering in 2025. Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.


Right infringement ‘misunderstood’: Chief, court

documents


The matter was originally brought to court in 2024. That year, Manitoba granted 88 licenses to hunters for use in Pimicikamak’s territory, according to court documents.


Before 2024, 400 big game hunting licenses were distributed through its moose lottery annually, but it was cut down to 100 to account for the declining population.


Pimicikamak argued that this was done without consultation and infringes on the agreement made in 1977.


In 2022, it had already requested that licensed moose hunting cease in the area, as the depleting number of licenses “confirms that there is not an ‘overabundance of the species’ in the region,” and therefore prohibits the hunting from happening, according to the agreement.


The court matter, however, was dismissed in October 2025, when the judge concluded that the subject of Treaty rights must be done through a civil lawsuit.


The MWF also brought the matter to court, stating that the cut to licenses was unjustified, but was also dismissed. The organization has also appealed.


Monias told APTN that the application was “misunderstood.”


“We are appealing to make sure that we have the first priority, as Treaty 5. We also have the Northern Flood Agreement that … clearly states in black and white that, when there’s a decline of the moose population, that we have a priority over those hunting areas,” he said. “And that’s the problem. They’re not following their own agreement and they’re not following their own Treaty.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Tusaajiapik elders home residents being relocated to Montreal
content:
Residents of Kuujjuaq’s Tusaajiapik elders home are being relocated to private facilities in a Montreal suburb 1,500 kilometres south.


The move, in response to technical issues with the building,

 was announced in a joint statement issued Wednesday and signed by Larry Watt, Ungava Tulattavik Health Center’s executive director, and Jennifer Munick-Watkins, Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services executive director.


“Transfers have begun

and will continue until all residents have been safely relocated,” the release stated.


The relocation is part of a three-way agreement that also includes Argyle Inc.’s long-term housing and care centre, a private seniors home in the Montreal suburb of Pointe-Claire.


“The agreement aims to provide for a safe, caring and culturally sensitive living environment, including

occasional access to traditional food and the support of three Inuit workers,” Wednesday’s statement continued.


Once all residents have been relocated, Tusaajiapik will close.


Watt and Munick-Watkins were both

out of town on Thursday and unavailable to comment, staff at their respective organizations said.


In Kuujjuaq, a

preliminary study is underway to assess the feasibility and scope of

bringing Tusaajiapik up to current standards, the release said.

A cost

 estimate is anticipated later this winter.


Tusaajiapik experienced “technical” issues with the building’s heating system, causing management to look into relocation options

last April

 for 13 elders, 10 of whom were described at the time as in wheelchairs or bedridden.


Last spring, the elders home employed 35 staff members, including nurses, social workers and personal care attendants.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Tk̓emlúps, community gathers to ‘reclaim our space’ and denounce white nationalism
content:
At the same site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc on Sunday, more than 100 Secwépemc people and their allies returned to the area two days later to reclaim the space. They drummed, sang and prayed to cleanse the spot, which is located a few hundred metres away from the former Kamloops Indian Residential School.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Content warning: This article contains details about residential “schools.” Please read with care for your spirit.


On the eve of Orange Shirt Day, more than 100 people gathered in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc to cleanse and reclaim a site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred earlier this week.


For nearly three hours on Tuesday night, Secwépemc people and their allies drummed, sang and prayed — for the land and the people, and for all the families impacted by residential “schools.”


Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Ashley Michel from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc organized Tuesday’s gathering with four other Secwépemc (Shuswap) mothers.


After seeing images of a group of masked white nationalists circulating on social media early this week, she told IndigiNews that they felt they had to come together to create a safer place for their children, and to help ground the community ahead of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation — also known as Orange Shirt Day — on Sept. 30.


“We’re all mothers. We don’t want our children growing up in a world like this. We brainstormed, and we just wanted to come together and cleanse the area,” said Michel, who is the owner of Four Generations Creations.


The organizers of Tuesday’s gathering in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc. From left to right: Ashley Michel, Cam Gottfriedson, Morning-Star Peters, Stephanie Lindley and Willow Peters.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


“We wanted to start things off in a good way and reclaim our space – take back our area and make it safe again. Especially for our children and our survivors.”


The group of about two dozen white nationalists were seen at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc reserve lands early Sunday morning. They hid their faces behind white masks and held a flag with the message “got bones?” — with images that quickly gathered outrage online.


The space where the group had gathered is a few hundred metres away from the former Kamloops Indian Residential School (KIRS) site and is located on the institution’s former grounds, which originally spanned 360 acres. 


At the same site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc on Sunday, more than 100 Secwépemc people and their allies returned to the area two days later to reclaim the space.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


In 2021

, leadership at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc revealed that they had identified evidence of 215 unmarked graves on the site, which unleashed a national reckoning about children’s deaths at the institutions.


“Sunday was just an example of what we at Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc are facing on a daily basis; on a weekly basis; on a monthly basis,” said Jeanette Jules, a Secwépemc knowledge keeper who helps manage the First Nation’s Le Estcwicwéy̓ (the missing children from KIRS) case. 


“Since 2021, we’ve kept emails, texts, phone messages. Some of them are really disturbing and disgusting.”


Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc Kúkwpi7 (Chief) Rosanne Casimir

said on Sunday

 that the group have ties to a group called Second Sons Canada, who are “linked to white supremacist and white nationalist ideology.”


“That blackness that they brought — that heaviness that they brought — is being lifted,” said Jules.


On Monday

, Tk̓emlúps RCMP said in a press release that they are investigating the incident. They described the masked men and their activities as “a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for their actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division.”


Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


A ceremony was also held by chief and council Monday evening …

author: Admin101
title: “A Dense Web of Solidarity”: How Chicago Public School Workers Defend Students Against ICE
content:
ICE’s invasion of Chicago during Operation Midway Blitz sparked a range of organized community responses, from rapid response teams


to fighting detentions at Broadview ICE Facility.


In this interview, Heather, a teacher with Chicago Public Schools (CPS) and the Chicago Teachers Union (CTU), reflects on their organizing experiences during that wave of struggle. Drawing on their work in school and supporting a picket line in the Little Village neighborhood, they describe building and mobilizing sanctuary teams while connecting immigrant defense to worker struggle.


This ground-floor recollection shows self-organization in the face of fear, few options for durable collective infrastructure, and uncertainty as to what the deportation siege might bring. It practically outlines the importance of solidarity and connecting struggles across sectors and sites. As the leadership of ICE/Border Patrol continues to change,


bringing a lower-key (and successful

) tactical shift, we must revisit our approach. This interview provides insights to apply to future struggles against ICE, Border Patrol, and whatever other forms of domination capital and the State throws at us.


Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): Tell us how you learned about

Operation Midway Blitz

. What was the sense at your school site and in your district?


Heather:

 Even before Midway Blitz, immigrant rights organizers in our union had run a training series, during the first Trump administration, about building sanctuary teams in the workplace. Our union also won “sanctuary” language in our contract during a strike in 2019, which set an institutional precedent to turn away ICE whenever legally possible. So, smaller groups of more active members were preparing, even before the surge began. 


After, there was a long lead up of news stories where the Trump administration was threatening and attempting to deploy the National Guard, threatening more ICE activity, etc. Our union was already seeing how the National Guard was harassing Black youth in Washington, D.C., and how ICE racially profiled people so blatantly, so among the more active members of our union, we were interpreting this as a direct threat to basically every student and family of color in our school district. During this lead-up, some federal agents showed up at a public elementary school wanting to see a student, and the workers and administrators successfully turned them away, which put the threat and the possibility of defeating it in everyone’s minds. It later came out that it was actually Secret Service agents trying to question the elementary schooler about social media posts, but that didn’t change anything for anyone. So when Midway Blitz began, parents and workers I knew were already fired up to do something about it.


BRRN:


How did you and other public school workers prepare for the potential of ICE deployments to your sites?


Heather:

At my school, we pulled together a “sanctuary team” that included myself, a security guard, the English Learner Program Teacher (ELPT), and other interested teachers and support staff. I took point on gathering all the resources and examples from my union’s trainings to share with the team. The ELPT had relationships with some of our most vulnerable families, so she was on distributing know-your-rights information to them, and other interested staff were going to do the same to families they had connections with. The security guard is responsible for watching our school’s entrance and he was the only one looped in with our administrators’ implementation of district-wide guidance. At times when the administration delayed implementing the district’s guidance at our school, the security guard was able to push them along, as well as fill in the sanctuary team on any gaps in their plan.


As a sanctuary team, we never had a set plan about how exactly we would respond if ICE showed up. Based on if ICE showed up during recess, drop-off, normal class, after-school, the front or back entrance, etc. our response would have to be completely different. We followed the advice from case studies we got at union trainings: go over general best practices, distribute know-your-rights and rapid response hotline information as widely as possible, think of different response options, and be prepared to communicate quickly if ICE shows up.


Some coworkers and I also flyered parents after school a few times with legal resources, info on the district policy’s protections for …

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Activists Are Pushing Cities and Companies to Cancel Parking Contracts With ICE
content:
The Trump administration’s abduction and deportation machine is multifaceted. There are clear-cut components — agents, shackles, and jails — and less obvious, although no less essential, ones — cars and parking spaces.


In an effort to impede the attacks on immigrants, mayors of some of the country’s largest cities, including

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

,

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson

, and

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu

, have issued executive orders

banning Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

 from using city-owned parking lots and properties.


But even in cities where mayors have banned ICE from using government-owned properties, ICE still has free reign to contract with private companies. After the federal agency

posted a notice

 seeking “Surge Parking” in 14 cities, including Boston, Wu

released a public letter

 to

local parking garage and lot owners

, warning them that if ICE were “to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region.”


“Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston,”

she wrote

. “In the face of escalating attacks on cities across the country, we have repeatedly seen that the strongest defense is solidarity.”


In the Boston suburb of Burlington, Massachusetts, Bearing Witness New England has been holding weekly protests outside ICE’s Boston Field Office, where people are

held for days

 in inhumane conditions. Activists say ICE has been keeping its vehicles in a nearby parking lot owned by local developer National Development.


According to a report by

NPR

 affiliate

WBUR

, the company sent a letter to local activists in February, stating that ICE vehicles were being “improperly parked” in its parking spaces, and that it had “reached an arrangement with ICE that they would no longer park their vehicles on our property.”


However, the company also said that the government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), has

rights to use the garage

 and the company does not have authority over how the FAA parcels out parking spaces to other federal agencies, according to

WBUR

’s report.


Nathan Phillips, a Boston University professor who organizes with the Burlington-area coalition

Building Up Resilience Networks (B.U.R.N.)

, says ICE has continued to park in sections of lots National Development leases to the FAA that exceed what the lease allows.


Protests that target parking garages are “throwing sand in the gears” of ICE’s deportation and abduction machine, he says.


“So much of their operation depends on logistics of transport and travel,” Phillips told

Truthout

. “It’s human trafficking, and so if we can go after the trafficking, the means by which they’re doing this, that can have a really effective impact.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


Fellow B.U.R.N. activist Josh Model says National Development’s recent actions contradict its public image as a

philanthropic company

 committed to improving communities.


“National Development Corporation, which, as a local developer, likes to promote that they’re cognizant of community needs and give to charity and all these nice things,” but they’re “letting ICE stage kidnappings” from their property, said Model.


While the government spending website,

usaspending.gov

, only lists 12 active contracts for parking spaces, as of September 28, the true number of parking lots that ICE uses is likely much higher, said Model. It’s difficult to untangle where ICE is parking, in part, because many of the contracts are not with ICE, but through another federal agency, the

General Services Administration

 (GSA), he said. The GSA manages government buildings and real estate, and owns or leases space in more than 8,300 buildings, according to an

explainer

 on the agency published by the Congressional Research Service.


In the case of National Development, ICE is using parking leased by the GSA for the FAA, according to Model.


Of the 12 contracts found on usaspending.gov, two were with the Philadelphia Parking Authority (PPA). The

PPA website

 states that, among other responsibilities, it coordinates “the efforts of public agencies concerning parking” and establishes and operates public …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Lili Reinhart Wants To Adapt a Lesbian Vampire Novella — Let Her!
content:
feature image photo by Emma McIntyre / Staff via Getty Images

Bisexual baddie Lili Reinhart has been on a press tour for her new film, The Love Hypothesis, and I’ve been really enjoying her interviews. The film seems to be the CLASSIC fake dating trope come to life — in fact, the book it’s based on started as Star Wars fanfic! — and despite the movie being seemingly extremely heterosexual, on this tour, she has been quick to remind interviewers and fans that she’s queer. She has also said she hopes in her next project is gay. (Fingers crossed!)

In one video interview she says, “I’m instantly way more interested in doing a movie if my character is a little gay,” she continued. “Because I’m a little gay.” She also reads a comment about being one of “the five pillars of bisexuality with preference to women” and she called it an honor.

In that same interview, she also mentioned that she’s trying to get a film adaptation of a lesbian vampire novella made but that Hollywood seems “too afraid” to make it. She also wonders aloud who WOULDN’T want to make it, a sentiment I agree with. The general assumption people have been making is that it would be an adaptation of the 1872 novella Carmilla, which the popular webseries starring Natasha Negovanlis and Elise Bauman was based on, and I think that would be fun if true. I personally think there can’t be too many adaptations of that novella. The gayer the better. In fact, I just read Hungerstone by Kat Dunn, which is one of a few retellings of that novella and offers a very different take than the webseries.

I, for one, am delighted that Lili keeps making her press tour about a heterosexual love story as queer as she can, and I’m glad she’s using it to pitch her idea. I really hope someone with the means is paying attention and can pick it up and let her run with it.

In my opinion, there’s no such thing as too many lesbian vampire adaptations in general. When is someone going to make a Bury Our Bones in the Midnight Soil miniseries? A movie version of A Long Time Dead, anyone? Let’s get all the lesbian vampires out here while we’re at it. Tis the season!

You can watch the full video interview here.

author: Kevin Carson
title: Ruthanna Emyrs, A Half-Built Garden, Tor 2022
content:
Recensione a cura di

Kevin Carson

. Originale:

A Half-Built Garden, by Ruthanna Emrys (Tor 2022)

, del 29 luglio 2026. Traduzione italiana di

Enrico Sanna

.


A Half-Built Garden

 è una storia di contatto alieno ben congegnata, dalla trama avvincente, cose che da sole fanno una piacevole lettura. Come forse saprà chi ha già letto altre mie recensioni, quando recensisco storie di fantascienza ambientate in un futuro prossimo utopico, libero e postcapitalista, il mio interesse riguarda anche come questo mondo è strutturato. Un peccatuccio che condivido con Auden che scrive ispirandosi alla bibbia.


Siamo negli anni 2080, dopo l’Età delle Turbolenze di metà secolo, e il mondo emerge dalle rovine del capitalismo per creare una nuova, tollerabile società.


La principale istituzione di governo è la watershed network, una federazione di istituzioni locali autogestite grossomodo corrispondenti alle bioregioni, comprendente gran parte della popolazione e delle risorse mondiali. L’equilibrio di potere è il risultato di una rivoluzione perlopiù nonviolenta iniziata una o due generazioni prima e finita verso il 2050: una serie di boicottaggi, sabotaggi e altre azioni dirette spingono le aziende economiche a rinchiudersi in enclave in alto mare. La vicenda è narrata attraverso gli occhi di un abitante della Chesapeake Watershed, che ricorda quando i suoi genitori “mettevano i primi sensori vietati nel fiume Potomac e barricavano le fabbriche per imporre la volontà collettiva della nascente rivoluzione dandelion.”


Le aziende sono perlopiù “padroni miliardari e dipendenti servi ammassati dietro il filo spinato nelle loro isole artificiali.” Tranne “qualche convertito e visitatore”, gli abitanti sono “i discendenti delle persone arrivate con il loro fondatore: dipendenti e sodali che preferivano scappare dall’apocalisse piuttosto che unirsi in comunità e evitarla.”


Le enclave aziendali sono circondate da “filo spinato” evidentemente imposto dalle watershed durante la rivoluzione. “Finalmente abbiamo vietato le aziende. Mio padre e altri, che hanno dato vita alla prima rete del cambiamento, hanno operato per fermarle.” La rivoluzione “limita la produzione di CO

2

 per contenere il riscaldamento climatico bloccando i trasporti quando si supera il limite.” Le aziende, “refrattarie al cambiamento, … finiscono per barricarsi dietro il filo spinato in alcune isole artificiali…”


Esiliate nelle isole, gran parte delle aziende, che “già da tempo hanno perso ogni parvenza di legalità”, rifiuta qualunque riconoscimento ufficiale dalle watershed. Inviano osservatori ai dialoghi sulla CO

2

, obbediscono tacitamente alle limitazioni dell’anidride e di altri inquinanti che le watershed, attori principali, impongono loro, e imbrogliano pensando di poter sfuggire ai controlli. Data la loro relativa debolezza, sono costrette a chiedere il permesso delle watershed consorziate quando l’impatto delle loro attività supera i confini.


Gran parte delle funzioni economiche delle società, tolte alcune zone che hanno ancora il monopolio del know-how, sono state rilevate dalle watershed. Comprese certe istituzioni industriali risalenti al periodo precedente, come il “MIT e l’Associazione di costruttori panasiatica” che sono “collegati alle reti dandelion”.


Le relazioni tra watershed e aziende sono generalmente da guerra fredda.


“Compriamo ancora da loro, saltuariamente… Cose che ci servono e che ancora non siamo riusciti a riprodurre con l’ingegneria a ritroso, oppure pratichiamo qualche scambio nella speranza di indurli a unirsi a noi. Quando succede, lasciamo che visitino le watershed, purché promettano di comportarsi bene.”


Nel loro rapporto con le aziende, il compito principale delle watershed è la gestione del declino: cercano di rilevarne le funzioni indispensabili rimanenti e mantenere i contatti così da indurle a cambiare la propria cultura, prevenendo ogni azione disperata di retroguardia che farebbe molte vittime.


Non scompariranno presto; dobbiamo continuare a parlare con loro o non cambieranno mai abbastanza da unirsi a noi…


“Abbiamo ancora bisogno di loro. Quando avevano il potere per poco non distruggevano il pianeta; ma fabbricano ancora delle parti importanti per la nostra infrastruttura. Loro pensano di aver bisogno di noi perché senza quelle esportazioni perderebbero la ragione d’esistere. In realtà, questo legame esile è la loro ultima possibilità. Ogni contatto serve a ricordare loro che c’è un’altra strada …

author: By Devon Cupery, Hannes Brunner, and Scott Russell, Contributors
title: Canadian Oil Giant Enbridge Builds Unauthorized Pipeline Bypass Following 1.3 Million Gallon Spill
content:
Saxon, WI – The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (DNR) repeatedly requested Enbridge keep its

Line 5

 pipeline shut down following the largest oil and gas spill in state history on Aug. 25. Enbridge defied the requests. Without receiving the required permits, it built a new pipeline to bypass the rupture and restarted Line 5’s operations.


Enbridge’s actions raise serious questions about the state’s ability to regulate large, multinational corporations and its willingness to enforce its permits.


Bad River Tribal Chair Liz Arbuckle asked DNR officials if the permits meant anything at all: “What are the consequences if they are violated?”


Arbuckle said the DNR representatives gave evasive responses. They told tribal leaders they are continuing to work with Enbridge in the permitting process. The DNR would not answer whether they would issue Enbridge retroactive permits for the bypass work.


DNR Sec. Karen Hyun and Wisconsin Governor Tony Evers have criticized Enbridge’s conduct, but so far they have stopped short of meaningful enforcement action, such as revoking permits or taking legal action. 


Aerial view of Enbridge’s unauthorized pipeline bypass and the Aug. 25 spill location in Saxon, WI. The site is four miles south of Lake Superior. Photo contributed by Devon Cupery.


In a Sept. 9

letter to Enbridge

, Hyun said that Enbridge has a growing list of environmental harms and permit violations, “demonstrating disregard for the environment, human health, and the statutory authority of the department.” Hyun said Enbridge’s Line 5 reroute permit violations have caused “continued frustration and profound unease” for state officials and the people of Wisconsin. 


Sept. 14 aerial image of the Line 5 excavation pit where the pipeline spill occurred in Saxon, WI. Photo contributed by Devon Cupery.


Enbridge contractors remove semi truck at the excavation pit where the spill occurred. Photo contributed by Devon Cupery.


People living near the pipeline have been unsatisfied with the DNR’s construction oversight. Bad River Tribal Member Joe Bates and others have taken it upon themselves to keep an eye on things and make sure that spills and violations are promptly reported. It is worth noting that Bates’

drone footage

 of the spill made international headlines.


Enbridge’s spill site bypass required state permits to cross streams and wetlands. The DNR did not approve the work. Enbridge blocked state officials from accessing the rupture site for weeks, citing safety concerns. When the DNR got access to the site, the bypass was under construction.


The federal government imposed a no-fly zone for 20 days, preventing independent monitors from recording drone footage of the spill site. During this information blackout, the DNR and the community at-large were dependent on Enbridge’s self-reporting about spill impacts. The no-fly zone was lifted on Sept. 14, the day Enbridge restarted the flow of oil through Line 5. 


Line 5 released more than 1.3 million gallons of toxic gas liquids when an Enbridge contractor truck struck the pipeline at an excavation site on Aug. 25. Photo contributed by River Akemann.


Beth Wallace of the National Wildlife Federation criticized Enbridge’s lack of transparency at a recent press briefing. “Enbridge claims to have learned from the 2010 Kalamazoo oil spill, but [their recent actions show] that they have only escalated the ways in which they shut out local communities, and that is making communities less safe.”


Wallace urged Wisconsin officials and residents to take the issue seriously, calling attention to Enbridge’s “alarming escalation of federal preemption.” She referenced a federal case currently playing out in Michigan where “Enbridge is trying to destroy state rights to regulate [projects] of this nature.”


Enbridge has received strong criticism from other state and Tribal leaders.


Enbridge’s Line 3 construction in Minnesota

ruptured several artesian aquifers

. The company withheld information from the state about its first breach for months. Minnesota DNR Commissioner Sarah Strommen

said

 in a media release that “Enbridge’s actions are clear violations of state law and also of public trust.”


On Sept. 9, Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer renewed her call for a Line 5 shutdown in the Straits of Mackinac, calling the pipeline a “ticking time bomb in the heart of the Great Lakes.” Whitmer urged outgoing Enbridge CEO Gregory Ebel to shut it down “within …

author: Eileen Flanagan
title: How to combat fear at the polls this November
content:
This article

How to combat fear at the polls this November

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


The ophthalmologist said he was going to touch my eyeball, then tilted my exam chair back in the darkness. I felt my body brace as movie torture scenes flashed through my mind. I noticed that I wasn’t breathing, so I practiced inhaling through my nose, and exhaling as steadily as I could for the rest of the exam.


Noticing our bodies and breathing intentionally may sound simple, but they are two of the practices that can keep us grounded when we are navigating scary or upsetting situations. As we approach a midterm election marred by threats of violence, I am practicing these skills as often as possible, not to suppress my feelings, but to be aware of how they are affecting me, so I can make conscious choices. 


Why staying grounded matters


The forces of authoritarianism want us to feel knocked off center by the many ways they are trying to keep people from voting. Trump administration officials continue to suggest that ICE, FBI or other federal agents could be sent to polling places. It’s important that election volunteers and voters stay grounded to avoid playing into their hands. One danger is that fearful voters will just stay home, whether or not the administration carries out their threats. Another danger is that we resist any government interference in ways that increase the chaos, which Trump would use to bolster his narrative that the left is the real threat.


Many national and local groups are hosting trainings to prepare people to protect our vote calmly and nonviolently. A widely used tool is the “

Election Defense Scenarios

” guide, which sketches out 18 possible threats and what people can do about them. Author

Daniel Hunter

 writes, “One of the clearest lessons from every scenario in this guide — and from democratic movements around the world — is this: Illegal and unjust orders only work if people comply with them.” He notes that a more subtle theme of the guide is handling fear. For example, those volunteering at the polls should make sure we do not become “vectors of fear” by spreading unfounded rumors.


Sign up for the latest updates.


Support Us


I learned the danger of rumors in 2020. Weeks before the presidential election, my friend Ingrid Lakey heard that the neo-fascist Proud Boys were coming to a park near her home in Philadelphia. Despite growing up as

George Lakey

’s daughter, and years of training for nonviolent direct action with Earth Quaker Action Team, or EQAT, Ingrid did not feel prepared to de-escalate armed militants if they wanted to stir up trouble. Neither did I, though given the times, we both wanted to increase our ability to handle scary situations. With two other friends from EQAT, we decided to show up, not to intervene, but to see what we could learn. 


We met early for a few minutes of silent Quaker worship and named our intention to observe what happened, including inside ourselves. We walked to the park early and watched hundreds of people arrive, none wearing MAGA hats. When the crowd’s energy became frenzied, we asked people nearby what was happening and were told there was a Proud Boy with a bat. Later we heard it was a hockey stick, or maybe a gun. 


The four EQAT members helped each other to assess what was actually happening rather than get caught up in the fearful energy. In the end, the Proud Boys never actually showed up, but the rumor of their presence led a small crowd to chase a man into his car. Within a few days, a video of his window being smashed got millions of views on conservative social media.


If a similar video emerges this election season, there is no doubt that Trump and the media that support him would use it to claim that leftists are the true threat to the vote, distracting from his many efforts to stop people from voting. Even if armed agents do show up near polling places, managing our fear will help us choose responses that will aid us both in court and in the court of public opinion. 


If Election Day turns out to be relatively uneventful — if our fear was the point, and the armed men never show — preparing ourselves for the worst-case scenarios will build nonviolence skills and relationships between organizations. Both will be important in the work ahead, no matter who wins the midterms.    


We have more experience than we realize


The good news is that many more Americans have learned the value of …
