title: Ephéméride des luttes : 30 septembre
content:
Dans l'éphéméride des luttes du 30 septembre, la belle ville de Naples nous met sur une voie intéressante pour penser l'avenir, et peut-être bien le présent : l'insurrection populaire, antifasciste et radicale.


1943 :

 Fin des quatre journées de Naples : l'occupant nazi est définitivement chassé de la ville par la population napolitaine après quatre jours d'insurrection.


1964 :

 En Colombie, création des FARC, qui existent toujours aujourd'hui et ont récemment annoncé le cessez-le-feu définitif.


1970 :

 A Puerto Rico, des manifestant-e-s brûlent plus de 1400 formulaires de conscription au service militaire.


1971 :

 En Irlande du Nord, deux membres de l'IRA 'Officielle' (OIRA) meurent dans l'explosion prématurée d'explosifs qu'ils confectionnaient.


1977 :

 - Arrestation à Paris de Klaus Croissant, ancien avocat des membres de la Fraction Armée Rouge allemande.


 A Rome, le militant de Lotta Continua Walter Rossi est assassiné par des fascistes, sous les yeux de la police : un groupe d'une quinzaine de fascistes avance dissimulé derrière un fourgon de police vers un groupe de jeunes d'extrême-gauche et commencent à tirer en arrivant à leur hauteur, touchant Rossi à la nuque. Le fourgon de police tourne à l'angle et part sans intervenir. Une manifestation sera ensuite organisée contre la présence des fascistes dans le quartier et leur protection par la police, qui sera réprimée par cette même police, tandis qu'un bar de fascistes est attaqué, un autre brûlé, et que des voitures personnelles de militants d'extrême-droite sont incendiés. Un début d'incendie se déclare également devant le local du MSI, le parti fasciste d'où étaient venus les tueurs.


1981 :

 A Carmaux, le groupe libertaire '

Les Artilleurs du Grand Soir

' fait sauter la statue de Jean Jaurès en soutien à la grève de la faim de prisonniers.


1999 :

 Au Japon, accident nucléaire dans l'usine de traitement d'uranium de Tokaimura.


2009 :

 En Suisse, près de Zurich, un groupe signant 'Azione Rivoluzionaria' incendie un véhicule de luxe en soutien au prisonnier anarchiste Marco Camenisch.


2014 :

 A Mexico, plusieurs véhicules du corps de sécurité de l'université sont incendiés pour leur rôle dans la surveillance qu'ils exercent pour le système judiciaire et en solidarité avec les prisonniers anarchistes.


2017 :

 A Göteborg en Suède, de violents affrontements ont lieu quand une contre-manifestation antifasciste s'est opposée à des néonazis qui tentaient d'organiser une manifestation dans la ville, ces derniers étant protégés par la police.


 Au Kurdistan Turc, près du village de Ziyaret (région de Lice et Diyarbakir), un sergent et un sergent-chef de l'armée turque sont enlevés après avoir été arrêtés à un barrage du PKK.

 A Assemini en Sardaigne, une grue d'une entreprise qui collabore activement aux chantiers de l'armée sur l'île

est incendiée

.


Voir

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 30 septembre.

author: Equality Now
title: California finally passes law banning child marriage
content:
30th September 2026


California finally passes law banning child marriage


14 min read


Press Releases


End harmful practices


United States


After years of legislative setbacks, survivors and campaigners celebrate California setting the legal age of marriage at 18 years old without exception.


Sacramento, California, September

 30,

 2026 –

California has finally banned child marriage. After nearly a decade of campaigning by

Unchained At Last

 along with survivors, grassroots organizations, and human rights organizations such as

Equality Now

, lawmakers have passed

Bill AB-1267

, establishing 18 as the minimum legal age of marriage without exception. The law closes a longstanding loophole that allowed children of any age to marry with parental consent and judicial approval.


The victory is a milestone for girls’ rights and for advocates who watched reform efforts repeatedly falter for almost a decade.


Sara Tasneem, a child marriage survivor who campaigned for the change, explained, “Seeing this legislation finally cross the finish line after nine years of advocacy will bring tears of both joy and pain. Reliving our trauma year after year has been exhausting, but survivor advocates have poured their hearts and souls into this fight to ensure the next generation is protected from the harms of child marriage. 


“This historic milestone is a testament to the relentless, collaborative efforts of everyone who refused to give up on protecting children,” said Tasneem.


California was one of only three U.S. states with no minimum marriage age 


Until now, California law allowed a child of any age to marry with the written consent of just one parent, even a non-custodial parent, and judicial approval. This absence of a minimum marriage age left the state far behind national and international standards. Only Mississippi and New Mexico share this unfortunate distinction in the U.S., while just 2% of high-income countries and 4% of low-income countries globally have no legislated minimum age.


Limited legal rights of minors in California leave them unable to protect themselves from forced marriage. They cannot leave home, enter a domestic violence shelter, retain an attorney, or bring independent legal action. Marriage-based emancipation comes too late, changing a child’s legal status only after marriage and still without conferring full adult rights. 


California’s law also created risks beyond the state. Because federal spousal and fianc

é

 visa requirements defer to the marriage age of the couple’s intended state of residence, a California visa could be approved for a child of any age. This opened a pathway for trafficking disguised as marriage, letting U.S. citizen adults bring foreign child spouses into California, and non-U.S. citizen adults to marry California minors to gain legal status. 


The vast majority of child marriages involve girls wed to adult men. Unchained At Last, a survivor-led nonprofit organization dedicated to ending forced and child marriage across the U.S., estimates that in

California, roughly 34,875 girls were married

 between 2000 and 2021. 


How child marriage harms girls


Child marriage is a grave human rights violation

 with consequences reaching far beyond the wedding day. Girls married before 18 face far greater risks of physical, sexual, emotional, and financial abuse, early and unwanted pregnancies they may not control, and poor mental and physical health.


Child brides are more likely to drop out of school, curtailing their educational, employment and economic opportunities and deepening dependence on their spouses. These disadvantages can persist into adulthood, with survivors tending to earn less and experience greater economic insecurity and higher rates of poverty than those who marry as adults.


In 2023, the

United Nations Human Rights Committee specifically called on the U.S.

 to prohibit marriage under 18. California’s new law represents an important step toward that obligation.


Why did it take California so long to ban child marriage?


In 2017, when then-

State Senator Jerry Hill introduced the first bill to ban child marriage

, advocates expected California to lead. Instead came a years-long process of repeated bills, committee defeats, and amendments, alongside disagreements among women’s and girls’ rights organizations.


Legislation was substantially amended in 2018, leaving a loophole that let the practice continue. Subsequent attempts …

title: Against male violence and male domination
content:
An extremely interesting march will take place in Amed today, 30 September. Perhaps it would be more accurate to call it a march without precedent, or one of very few of its kind. Men will march against male violence. Through this march, they will protest the dominant male violence directed against women. Until now, women have organized marches and rallies to protest male violence against women. Some men who had educated themselves on the basis of women's freedom would occasionally participate in these demonstrations and marches. Now, however, men themselves are organizing and carrying out a march to protest male violence against women. And beginning in Amed, which is known as the “capital of democracy.” In this way, the spirits of the many Gülistan Doku, Rojin Kabaiş and little Narin Güran, who were murdered by dominant masculinity, may find at least some consolation.


Undoubtedly, the fact that such a historically significant action is taking place in Amed also carries great meaning. This action demonstrates the level of development and strength attained by the Kurdish Freedom Revolution. It reveals that the essence of this revolution is, in fact, a Women's Freedom Revolution. Once again, it proclaims to the entire country and the world that Amed is a pioneering city of such a revolution. It calls on everyone to join the social revolution based on women's freedom and directed against dominant masculinity.


Some people who are sworn enemies of Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] and the PKK, which have spearheaded the Kurdish identity and freedom revolution, claim that this struggle, which has continued uninterrupted for 50 years, “has achieved nothing.” It is particularly noticeable that such statements have increased since Leader Apo's 27 February 2025, Peace and Democratic Society Process. According to them, the war waged for 50 years was supposedly for nothing, and all the blood, sweat and suffering were wasted! Yet the march scheduled to take place in Amed on September 30 clearly demonstrates that the struggle waged over the past 50 years, the blood shed and the suffering endured have enabled the Kurds to experience one of the greatest and most meaningful freedom revolutions in history. It has transformed Kurdish society, where patriarchy and feudal relations were among the most deeply entrenched, into a pioneer of the Women's Freedom Revolution. So much so that Kurdish men, who under reactionary notions of honor and custom once considered every form of oppression, violence and murder against women acceptable, are now marching against all of this so that women can live freely and equally. Can there be a greater or more meaningful development in the cause of freedom? Can there be a more profound and meaningful transformation toward liberation? If these people are not sworn enemies of freedom, why have they been attacking this development and transformation for decades?


One might argue that if men had to march against male violence in Amed, then male oppression and violence against women is still continuing. Undoubtedly, this argument is correct in one respect. The consequences of dominant male violence in Amed and other cities appear in the news every day. Women struggle every day against this dominant male violence and the massacres it produces. Indeed, on the very day the planned action was announced, the DEM Party's Women's Spokesperson's Office also issued a statement condemning this male violence. Of course, all of this is one side of the matter. The other side is that people are refusing to submit to this dominant male oppression and violence. The struggle being waged by women in Kurdish cities, particularly Amed, against dominant male violence and killings is now being joined by a men's movement that is beginning in Amed. Yes, dominant masculinity still exercises oppression and violence, but women and men are also engaged in a highly conscious and organized struggle for freedom against it. This struggle is what offers hope for a free and equal life in the future.


Of course, we cannot simply dismiss what is happening as “a march” and move on. Yes, on September 30, men will march for women's freedom, but this is part of the historic Women's Freedom Revolution that is advancing with tremendous force, and it is one of its most meaningful aspects. Looking back at recent history, one can see with the naked eye how far things have come. Let us not forget that this protest march by men against male violence …

author: Akoko Akech
title: Homa Bay: The Road to Afgoonistan and the Van-goons of Democracy
content:
The political violence that characterized Linda Mwananchi’s forceful entry into Homa Bay and earned the county online mimetic mockery and nicknames such as Afgoonistan or Yemen didn’t begin in either the dust bowls of its lakeside town of Nyandiwa or the dusty roads of the county’s Ruma National Park, the route that the Linda Mwananchi entourage took to the heart of Homa Bay County, Asego ka DC, the administrative headquarters. 


It began in India with the intestate death of Raila Odinga. For over two decades, Raila’s charismatic leadership and competitive presidential ambition singularly disciplined both leaders and voters in Nyanza. Although it was the magnet that attracted disciplined ideologues, crass opportunists, and fellow travellers in Nyanza’s politics, it held competing egos and political ambitions in check. It also maintained a delicate balance within ODM: the contradictory or opposed politics of protest against the powers that be and the politics of protecting the powers that be, as the case may be, as well as the Luo elite politics of righting the wrongs of Kenya’s postcolonial state primarily as a national common good and only secondarily as a particular Luo ethnic good.    


Raila is dead. It is the end of an epoch. A new leadership struggles to be born in his Nyanza strongholds. Now it is time for monsters: castration angst, misogyny, sexism, mythical histories of Luo origins and migration, the bitter historical memories of postcolonial betrayals, elite and ethnic tribulations. Violence. 


Homa Bay’s road to “AfGoonistan” on 16

th

 August began when James Orengo, Siaya governor and a Linda Mwananchi advocate who is also popularly known by nicknames such as Nyatieng’, wuod nya Mayanga, or “the walking constitution”, took to the sun roof of his car and made an incendiary, vulgar, and sexist speech in May.  


In a speech “full of sound and fury, dignifying nothing” in Kadongo, the far-flung fecund highlands of Homa Bay County where peasants grow some of Kenya’s sweetest pineapple and sweet potatoes, Orengo fired the first sexist and vulgar salvo against Homa Bay governor Gladys Wanga, in Dholuo. True to his Nyatieng’ moniker, Orengo hit Governor Wanga below the belt. He said: 


“Dhi nyis nya Wangaya, ni an ja siasa ma ok onego otug godo. Ase neno siasa ma opogore gi siasa ma oseneno. An ok alony siruaru ni ngato. An ok alony siruaru ni ngato. Ma saa duto oloso mana e nyinga, an ma enana ni, an ok nindo koda, an ema anindo gi ngato. Koso awacho ma rach? Koso awacho ma rach? Moko wacho ni Orengo otii, sani e koro ka aroch, sani abith. To ka oneno ni ati, obi otem, one mach, koro e ka obiro neno. Kadongo Oyee! Kasipul, Oyee!”


“Go tell Nya Wangaya [Gladys Wanga] that I am a seasoned politician she should not joke with. The kind of politics I have experienced is different from what she has seen. I do not strip my panties for anyone. I do not strip my panties for anyone. All the time she talks about me. As you can see, no one sleeps with me, I sleep with someone. Have I said something bad? Have I said something bad? Some say Orengo is old, yet I have now rejuvenated. I am virile. But if she thinks that I’m old, let her try, she will see fire, then she will know. Kadongo Oyee! Kasipul Oyee!”


Although Orengo had addressed Governor Wanga simply as “Nya Wangaya”, ordinarily a term of endearment, there was nothing endearing or romantic about his invitation. Orengo’s speech in Dholuo rhymed with Catherine MacKinnon’s syntax of “Man fucks woman”, an expression that captures the contemptuous diminution of women to mere sex objects and women’s bodies to sites where violent men perform their patriarchal heterosexual fantasies.  


If Orengo often punctuates his political speeches with words such as

“dhako wadwa, mon wetena”

 – “fellow woman, fellow women” – to signal symbolic identification with the womenfolk, when challenged by a woman leader in the ODM leadership struggles, Orengo reached for the phallus. The walking constitution’s velvet gloves were off. He was revelling in the privilege of the phallus, to cheers from the crowd surrounding his car. He came to Homa Bay to express a strong patriarchal will to power.


Orengo’s vulgar, sexist speech in Homa Bay County – a county that not only elected the first woman governor in Nyanza and chair of the ODM party, but also boasts three elected women members of parliament out of eight constituencies – signified the end of an era: the end of civil politics of …

author: David Swanson
title: Parliamentary Dialogue on Peace in Cameroon on the Occasion of International Peace Day 2026
content:
Africa, International Day of Peace, Nonviolent Activism

By Guy Feugap, World BEYOND War’s Africa Organizer, September 27, 2026

On the occasion of the International Day of Peace, celebrated on September 21, 2026, a parliamentary dialogue focused on peace, social cohesion, and the protection of populations was held in Cameroon at the invitation of the United Nations in Cameroon. The meeting, held at the National Assembly headquarters, brought together representatives from Parliament and the Government, civil society organizations, and various stakeholders and partners committed to promoting peace and combating gender-based violence, femicide, and infanticide. Cameroon, already mired in armed conflicts, is now characterized by growing insecurity for people in their daily lives. Unfortunately, institutions have proven unable to prevent and respond to the various forms of violence threatening the population.

The first session of the parliamentary dialogue, dedicated to Parliament’s role in promoting peace, focused on how the National Assembly, the Senate, and members of Parliament can use their constitutional functions and public leadership to contribute to a peaceful environment. Discussions focused in particular on inclusive dialogue, nonviolent political participation, prevention and early warning, accountability in political communication and information, as well as the protection and inclusion of women, youth, people with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups. Peaceful dispute resolution and dialogue were also identified as important elements of peacebuilding.

The second session was devoted to strengthening prevention and response to gender-based violence, femicide, and infanticide. Introduced by the Vice President of the National Assembly and the United Nations Advisor on Peace and Development, among others, the dialogue addressed these forms of violence as issues involving human rights, protection, justice, public health, governance, and peace. The discussions shed light on a troubling situation. The rise in certain forms of crime and violence is an additional cause for concern. Femicide and infanticide—including in places where women and children should be protected, such as homes and schools—illustrate the scale of the challenges facing Cameroonian society. Civil society reaffirmed its role in educating and raising awareness among the public, as well as in advocating for a legal framework to better prevent and punish these crimes. In this regard, World BEYOND War and WILPF Cameroon launched a letter-writing campaign addressed to the Prime Minister, Head of Government, to draw the authorities’ attention to the urgent need for strengthened action against femicides.

On the government’s side, it was noted that the process of drafting the bill on gender-based violence is at an advanced stage and that the text is nearly finalized. Parliamentary representatives, for their part, indicated that they are ready to review and vote on the bill as soon as it is officially submitted to them. This prospect was one of the key takeaways from the dialogue: the need to translate the concerns expressed by civil society and other stakeholders into concrete institutional and legislative measures. Beyond the adoption of a law, the discussions also highlighted the importance of a coordinated response encompassing prevention, reporting, referral of victims and survivors, protection, investigation, prosecution, justice, psychosocial support, and institutional coordination.

The parliamentary dialogue held on International Day of Peace 2026 thus brought together two dimensions that are often addressed separately: peacebuilding and the struggle against gender-based violence. For civil society organizations working on these issues, preventing femicides, infanticides, and other forms of violence is not merely a matter of justice or the protection of human rights. It also contributes to building a peaceful society, in which every person can live free from violence and where institutions fully assume their responsibility to protect. The organizations that participated in this session will continue to ensure that the commitments and discussions arising from this meeting are translated into concrete actions.

author: Unknown
title: Bakırhan Diyarbakır’da, Hatimoğulları Erzurum’da konuştu
content:
Halkların Eşitlik ve Demokrasi Partisi (DEM Parti) Diyarbakır İl Örgütü, 3’üncü Olağan Kongresini gerçekleştirdi.


Pervin Buldan: Somut adımların atılacağı bir sürece gireceğiz


23 Eylül 2026


ÇandAmed Kongre Merkezi’nde gerçekleştirilen kongreye, DEM Parti Eş Genel Başkanı Tuncer Bakırhan’ın yanı sıra çok sayıda siyasi parti ile sivil toplum örgütü temsilcisi katıldı. 


"Bedel verdiğimiz talepleri konuşacağız"


DEM Parti Eş Genel Başkanı Tuncer Bakırhan, "Henüz Kürtlerin demokratik haklarını, kayyımları, kimliğimizi, ana sütümüz gibi helal olan dilimizi konuşmadık. Bu birinci aşamayı başarıyla sonuçlandırabilirsek, ikinci aşamada mücadele ettiğimiz, emek verdiğimiz, bedel verdiğimiz talepleri konuşacağız” dedi.


Efkan Ala'dan süreç açıklaması: Alt kurullar çalışmalara başladı


18 Eylül 2026


"Kürtler yüz yıl sonra ilk defa menüde değil, masadadır" diyen Bakırhan, sözlerine şöyle devam etti:


"Eğer kıymetini bilirsek, doğru yürütebilirsek, bir birimizle uğraşmak yerine bizi reddeden, inkar eden Ortadoğu’daki bu rejimlere karşı demokratik haklarımızı inançlı ve güçlü şekilde savunabilirsek, menüde olan biz olmayız. Sayın Öcalan’ın Kürtleri menüden kaldırarak masaya koyan süreci başlatması kıymetlidir, önemlidir. 13 Eylül’de Sayın Öcalan’la yapılan görüşmede, Sayın Öcalan heyetimize, ‘Artık fazla gecikmeden karşılıklı adımlar atılmalı ve kurullar karşılıklı çalışmaya başlamalı’ dedi. Bizde diyoruz; artık gecikmeyin, neyi bekliyorsunuz? En başta da bu sürecin mimarı olan Sayın Öcalan’ın yaşam, iletişim koşullarını düzenleyin. Her gün birileri, ‘İmralı’da şöyle bir görüşme yapılmış’ deniliyor. Bu işin mimarı orada; kapıyı açın basın, sivil toplum örgütü gitsin. Gidip yerinde doğru bilgi almak daha iyi değil midir? Bu süreç sadece bir barış süreci değildir. Aynı zamanda demokratikleşme sürecidir. Bu sürecin karakteri olarak demokratikleşmeyi okuyoruz. Sürecin barıştan demokrasiye evrilmesi için, başta iktidar olmak üzere hepimizin çaba içinde olması gerekiyor."


Erdoğan’dan süreç açıklaması: "Barış ve istikrar olacak"


25 Ağustos 2026


"Cumhuriyet hareketi yaratacağız"


Bakırhan, şunları söyledi: “Barış ne demektir, kısaca anlatayım; barış hiçbir eve cenaze gitmemesi demektir, bir gencin yarınını planlamasıdır, insanların dilini, inancını özgürce yaşamasıdır, silahların sustuğu yerde demokrasi ve hukukun devreye girmesi demektir. O yüzden bu sürecin başarıya ulaşması gerekiyor. Bizim talip olduğumuz, istediğimiz rejimin adı demokratik cumhuriyettir. Demokratik cumhuriyet Kürdün, alevinin, ezilenin eşit şekilde onuruyla yaşadığı bir zemindir, sistemdir. Kayyımların, dil yasaklarının, özgürlüğü kısıtlayan uygulamaların olmadığı bir demokratik cumhuriyet hareketi yaratacağız."


Tülay Hatimoğlulları: Bu düzen böyle gitmez


DEM Parti Erzurum İl Örgütü, 2’nci Olağan Kongresi’ni gerçekleştirdi. Kongreye, Eş Genel Başkan Tülay Hatimoğulları ile çok sayıda yurttaş katıldı.           


Hatimoğulları, şunları söyledi: “Bugün Türkiye'de hangi kanalı açarsanız varlık fonu üzerinden gerçekleşen hırsızlık karşımıza çıkar. İlk defa bu kadar büyüklükte bir vurgunla karşı karşıyayız. İktidar ise sanki bu hırsızlık kendi ülkesinde yaşanmıyormuş gibi davranıyor ve soruları yanıtsız bırakıyor. Bunun sorumlusu çok net denetlemeyen kurumlar, önünü açan siyasiler ve iktidarın önünü açtığı yolsuzluk furyasıdır. Ülkeyi vurgunların merkezi haline getirdiler. İktidar bu vurgunu izliyor. Bu vurgunun başında iktidarın önceki dönemde bakanlık yapan birine dayanıyor. Ucu nereye dokunursa dokunsun araştırılmalı. Türkiye şuan yoksulluğun en dibini yaşayan ülkelerin başında. title: Kocaeli'de kadın cinayeti: Fatma Çiğil eski eşi tarafından katledildi
content:
Kocaeli'nin Körfez ilçesinde 54 yaşındaki İbrahim Ç. eski eşi 37 yaşındaki Fatma Çiğil'i sokakta ateşli silahla vurdu. Derince Eğitim ve Araştırma Hastanesine kaldırılan yaralı Çiğil müdahalelere rağmen kurtarılamadı.

Yerel basın, Fatma Çiğil'i Vadi Sokak'ta vurduktan sonra olay yerinden kaçan İbrahim Ç.'nin kısa süre önce cezaevinden çıktığını aktardı. Ses Kocaeli'nin haberinde saldırganın daha önce de Körfez Belediyesinde silahlı intihar girişiminde bulunduğu belirtildi.

Polis, cinayeti işleyen İbrahim Ç.'nin bulunması için çalışma başlattı.

Kadın Cinayetlerini Durduracağız Platformu verilerine göre 2026 yılında en az 256 kadın, erkekler tarafından katledildi. Ağustos ayında 22 kadın erkekler tarafından öldürülürken, 33 kadın da şüpheli şekilde ölü bulundu. Ağustos ayında işlenen kadın cinayetlerinden yüzde 64’ünde ateşli silah kullanıldı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Cameron Mitchell
title: ‘No Bystanders’ concert highlights violence against women, raises funds for charities
content:
Caitlin Davies with the support of Australian Femicide Watch, Socialist Alliance, Violent Butterfly Records and other activist groups organised a fundraising concert on September 5 to highlight and educate people about violence against women.

The mixed-bill hardcore concert, titled No Bystanders, heard from 14 local bands, which volunteered to allow ticket proceeds to go to relevant charities.

The all-ages concert included face painting for children and adults, provided by Rhee Brown, and merchandise stalls which lined the Royal Park Hall venue, between two stages.

Each band, hosting several mosh pits, drew an impressive crowd. The energy of the punk/metal music matched the anger felt towards the injustice women face.

The stories of women who have become victim to femicide were highlighted. The wall was filled with faces of women who had been killed by men from 2024 to 2026. The memorial allowed participants to write letters to be read by speakers affected by domestic violence.

Two women, in particular, were the focus of photo collages: Ebony Lee and Ali Lauren. Lee, a close friend of Davies, had her life taken earlier this year. Lauren, a local, was murdered last year by a conspiracy theory podcaster.

Davies said a fundraiser after Lee’s death had raised $46,000 for victims of male violence, and was one of the main inspirations behind No Bystanders.

Violence against women is reaching catastrophic levels. Australian Femicide Watch reports that 49 women and 19 children have been killed by male violence this year, and more than 1300 women and children have been killed since 2000.

Femicide has been exacerbated by the rise of reactionary “manosphere” influencers, such as Andrew Tate, whose profile big tech algorithms push to young men.

Attendees reflected on all the issues at a candlelit vigil towards the end of the night.

Erinn, another volunteer, read Davies’ speech: “We’re standing here surrounded by the faces of women whose lives were taken by violence. They weren't statistics. They were people. They were loved. They had families, friends, futures, whole lives that should never have been cut short. They should still be here.

“A while ago, we lost my two friends, Ebony and Tam, within six months of each other. Their life ended because of a lot of complicated reasons, and so much of that traces back to male violence and the fall-out of it. That kind of harm doesn’t stop in one moment. It keeps moving through people. It affects their mental health, their safety, their relationships, the way they cope, and the weight they have to carry.”

Davies said it is important to stand up against this violence. “What you walk past, you accept. That’s part of why I called this event No Bystanders. Because silence is not neutral. Looking away is not neutral. Grief on its own is not enough. If we actually want things to change, then we have to be willing to look at this clearly, call it what it is, and do something with that.”

The event raised $10,000, of which $8000 was donated to Australian Femicide Watch, and a further $2000 to ERICA Women’s Centre.

Davies told Green Left afterwards that she wanted the event to focus on encouraging young people to recognise the signs of sexual or domestic violence “so that kids can see what toxic relationships can turn into”.

author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: “Debemos pensar en una insurrección popular frente a los gobiernos fascistas”
content:
Por Mariángeles Guerrero


María Leonor Yonda es vicepresidenta del Coordinador Nacional Agrario (CNA) de Colombia. El CNA comenzó como un proceso de base en 2009; hoy nuclea a 50 organizaciones conformadas por jóvenes, campesinos y campesinas, pescadores y pescadoras y pueblos negros e indígenas de ese país. Tiene presencia en 24 de los 32 departamentos de Colombia y fue impulsora de los Territorios Agrarios Campesinos (Tecam), reconocidos por el gobierno de Gustavo Petro en 2024. El nuevo gobierno, de Abelardo de la Espriella, promete alianzas con los sectores concentrados de la economía y el recrudecimiento de la persecución a lideresas y líderes campesinos. Ante ese panorama,

“proponemos un modelo de vida opuesto al de la clase dominante, que ha ostentado el poder bajo la criminalización, con fuerzas como el paramilitarismo”

, asegura Yonda.


Entre las reivindicaciones del CNA están

 la recuperación y la permanencia en la tierra, la defensa del territorio y el ambiente, la agroecología, la soberanía alimentaria y la defensa de los derechos humanos

, a los que prefieren definir como

 “derechos de los pueblos”

. Es, en términos de la entrevistada, “una estrategia de lucha de clases, frente al capitalismo, al despojo y al extractivismo”.


Respecto a la injerencia estadounidense en América Latina, denunciada por observadores internacionales respecto a Honduras, Colombia y Argentina (por dar algunos ejemplos), reflexiona: “

No somos el patio trasero de Estados Unidos, somos la puerta delantera.

 Por eso es esta guerra mediática, esta narrativa que viene ganando el fascismo. Tenemos que poner nuestra inteligencia al servicio del movimiento social, cambiar la disputa ideológica y ser más ágiles en la comunicación. Los pueblos nos tenemos que juntar para cambiar esa batalla desde lo ideológico, desde la formación y desde lo organizativo”.


Las raíces del CNA se remontan al paro cafetero de 1997 llevado adelante en el centro del país, entre otros motivos, por las deudas que asediaban a los productores de café. En la memoria se inscriben además las movilizaciones de trabajadores caficultores del 2013-2014. La organización también encuentra su raigambre en la Asociación Nacional de Usuarios Campesinos, una de las primeras organizaciones campesinas colombianas, que data de los años 60. “Venimos de ese legado. Muchos padres y familias hacían parte de la Asociación y desde ahí surgimos”, afirma.


Oriunda de El Tambo y Argelia (localidad del Cauca, en el oeste de Colombia), explica que la apuesta política del Coordinador se enmarca en el internacionalismo, por eso confluyen en La Vía Campesina. La formación política del CNA tiene componentes de geopolítica y pone la lupa sobre cómo el imperialismo fue parte de la estrategia de guerra interna en Colombia, conflicto armado que lleva décadas y que intentó resolverse mediante el Acuerdo de Paz de 2016.


Según Yonda, el eje de acción prioritario del CNA

 es la movilización constante y la recuperación de tierras frente a las empresas que históricamente han despojado al campesinado

. En Colombia, para 2022, el uno por ciento de la población concentraba el 81 por ciento de la tierra, según Oxfam.


Foto: Coordinador Nacional Agrario de Colombia


El campesino: una identidad política negada, una palabra prohibida


El Estado colombiano firmó, en 2016, un Acuerdo de Paz con las Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia (FARC). Implicaba la deposición de las armas por parte de la guerrilla, pero también el compromiso estatal con reformas estructurales y políticas que mejoren las condiciones de vida en las zonas rurales, donde las FARC emergieron y tuvieron su mayor desarrollo. Entre los puntos del acuerdo, una de las claves era

la democratización de la tierra: la reforma agraria

.


El gobierno de Gustavo Petro (2022-2026) fue el que más avanzó respecto a la cantidad de hectáreas devueltas a las familias campesinas. Según la

Agencia Nacional de Tierras

, el ex presidente Juan Manuel Santos entregó 27.287 hectáreas e Iván Duque 32.614. Hasta fines de 2025, el gobierno de Gustavo Petro había gestionado la entrega de 700.000.


Si bien los crímenes contra líderes campesinos ocurrieron en todos los gobiernos, según datos del Instituto de Estudios para el Desarrollo y la Paz (Indepaz), desde que De la Espriella ganó las elecciones se registraron 61 campesinas, campesinos e indígenas asesinados. Por ejemplo, el 31 de agosto

title: Día de Acción Global por el acceso al Aborto Legal y Seguro
content:
Ante el Congreso de la Nación, colectivas y activistas feministas se manifestaron “para defender el derecho a decidir, el acceso a la salud sexual y reproductiva, la Educación Sexual Integral y todos los derechos conquistados gracias a nuestra lucha”.

Bajo la consigna “Educación sexual para decidir, anticonceptivos para no abortar y aborto legal para no morir”, la Campaña Nacional por el Derecho al Aborto Legal, Seguro y Gratuito junto a otras organizaciones y activistas realizó un pañuelazo en la Plaza del Congreso, denunciando el “vaciamiento sistemático de las políticas de salud sexual y (no) reproductiva” por parte del gobierno nacional de ultraderecha de Javier Milei.


Desde hace más de tres décadas, el 28 de septiembre se conmemora el Día de Acción Global por el Aborto Legal, una fecha que nació en América Latina y que cada año reactualiza la consigna por el derecho a decidir. Su origen se encuentra en 1990, cuando durante el V Encuentro Feminista Latinoamericano y del Caribe realizado en San Bernardo,  activistas de toda la región declararon el 28 de septiembre como Día por la Despenalización y Legalización del Aborto, a partir de una propuesta de la delegación brasileña que recuperó un antecedente histórico: ese mismo día de 1871, Brasil promulgó la Ley de Libertad de Vientres, que liberaba a los hijos de mujeres esclavizadas.


La sanción de la Ley 27.610 en 2020 convirtió a Argentina en referencia regional: la norma garantiza la Interrupción Voluntaria del Embarazo hasta la semana 14 y la Interrupción Legal del Embarazo en casos de violación o riesgo para la salud. Sin embargo, las organizaciones que convocan a la movilización advierten que, si bien la ley continúa vigente, el acceso efectivo al aborto enfrenta problemas de financiamiento, provisión de medicamentos y desigualdades territoriales. Entre las dificultades señaladas figuran recortes en políticas de salud sexual, dificultades en la provisión de anticonceptivos y medicamentos como misoprostol y mifepristona, y retrocesos en programas como el Plan ENIA.


En ese marco político, el presidente Milei volvió a atacar al feminismo y al aborto legal: frente a su público favorito, empresarios, responsabilizó a los sectores que impulsaron la legalización por la caída en la tasa de natalidad.


Desde las organizaciones feministas y sectores académicos se responde que la baja de la natalidad no se explica por la interrupción del embarazo, sino por causas económicas y sociales como la precarización laboral, la falta de vivienda y la sobrecarga de cuidados.

 se publicó primero en

title: Rencontre avec Sandeep Bakshi sur Frontières queer
content:
Jeudi 15 octobre à 19h30, rencontre avec Sandeep Bakshi pour la sortie de son livre Frontières queer, sexualité, colonialité, décolonialité. La rencontre sera animée par Zaid du collectif sud-asiatique/Brown antiraciste.


Le queer est-il seulement occidental

 

? Conçu au cœur même des Empires, son lexique est-il utile loin des métropoles et logiques coloniales

 

? Dans cet ouvrage, Sandeep Bakshi remet en question les généalogies admises du queer pour échapper aux instrumentalisations et aux normalisations dont il est l'objet.


Partant de pratiques et d'analyses des Suds, ce livre montre que, si les études et le militantisme queer ont produit des formes de pensée radicales, elles ne sont pas immunisées contre les a priori culturels, sociaux et raciaux. Le queer, lui aussi, a sa colonialité. Dès lors, c'est en adoptant une perspective décoloniale que le queer retrouvera toute la vigueur de son insurrection initiale, pour semer à nouveau le trouble.

title: TGEU contributes expertise to new guidance on SOGIE rights in detention
content:
TGEU served on the Expert Advisory Group for the publication Advancing SOGIE Rights in Detention: Promising Practices, a new guidance note published by the

Association for the Prevention of Torture


(APT). This included providing initial input on the project, reviewing a first draft during a consultation meeting in Geneva in March 2026, and providing expert feedback on an advanced draft.


The publication documents promising practices by governments, prison administrations, staff and oversight bodies to improve conditions for LGBTI people in detention. It pays particular attention to trans communities and highlights approaches that address the structural challenges faced by LGBTI people deprived of liberty.


The publication was presented during a dedicated session at the TGEU Trans Council in Ljubljana on 11 September 2026.

author: Bram Sable-Smith
title: Missouri’s Abortion Rights Face a Second Vote in Two Years
content:
Abortion returns to ballots in Missouri and other states as voters and lawmakers reshape post-Roe policies.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

After Missouri voters added abortion protections to the state constitution in 2024, Kelly McCoomb decided to keep her yard sign supporting the measure in the basement of her suburban St. Louis home.

Abortion access is important to McCoomb. She wants her daughter to grow up in a state where the option is available if needed, and the sign was a keepsake from the day Missourians voted to reverse the state’s near-total ban. McCoomb also couldn’t shake the feeling that she’d need to display the sign in her yard again soon.

“I have little faith in our Missouri government,” McCoomb said, sitting on her front porch.

Sure enough, just two years later, the state’s Republican-dominated legislature is asking Missouri voters to overturn the abortion protections they recently supported. The conflicting measures even have the same title: Amendment 3. But while a “yes” vote in 2024 supported adding protections to the state constitution, a “no” vote in 2026 would keep them. McCoomb covered the “YES” on her yard sign with a “NO” made from black duct tape before placing the sign back in her yard.

Voters will weigh in on abortion in Missouri, and three other states, in the November general election. Missouri is also one of two states voting on it for the second time since 2024. Nevada will vote again, too.

The spate of referendums comes after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned federal abortion protections with its 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, leaving each state to make its own abortion policy. The result has been a patchwork of state rules with varying degrees of bans or limitations, and even a series of “shield laws” in states where abortion remains legal that aim to protect providers from prosecution in states where it’s not.

“I just think there’s a constitutional crisis that’s coming,” said Kristi Hamrick, vice president of media and policy for the anti-abortion organization Students for Life Action.

“Can you have 50 state standards on whether or not a human being is a human being? Can you have 50 state standards on whether human beings have legal protection?” Hamrick said.

That patchwork of abortion protections is the reason Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom introduced the 2024 ballot measure to enshrine the state’s law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception into the state constitution, said Denise Lopez, president of the coalition.

The measure received strong support two years ago, with 64% of voters in favor. Nevada law requires two majority votes to enshrine constitutional amendments, so voters will need to support the expanded protection again in November for it to be enacted.

The Nevada ballot measure wouldn’t change the state’s existing law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception. But the proposal would make it more difficult to overturn abortion access, requiring voter approval of any new ban in two elections.

Lopez said Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom has been campaigning to ensure voters are still mobilized.

“Folks care about it,” she said. “They’re seeing what’s happening at the national level, and they want to make sure that whatever’s happening in our neighboring states, like Idaho and Utah, doesn’t happen here in Nevada.”

Idaho, where a ballot measure establishing abortion rights recently qualified to go before voters in November, has one of the strictest abortion bans in the country. Voters will decide whether state statute should allow abortion through fetal viability, the point when a fetus can survive after birth, which is generally considered to be around 24 weeks.

In Utah, abortion is allowed up to 18 weeks while legal challenges to the state’s ban continue.

In Virginia, where abortion is already allowed through two trimesters of pregnancy, until 28 weeks, voters will decide whether to amend their state constitution to codify those rights.

Missouri is the only state voting this year on removing abortion protections already on the books. The measure would repeal the 2024 amendment that guaranteed abortion access through fetal viability in the state and replace it with a ban on abortions with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, and pregnancies resulting from rape or incest. Yek ji parêzeran diyar kir ku beriya Lûtkeya NATOyê nêzîkî 100 kesî bi awayekî "tedbîr" hatine girtin û got ku Duru di çarçoveya van lêpirsînan de kesê dawî ye ku girtî maye.


Parêzer da zanîn ku bişopandina fîzîkî û qeydên di dosyayê de di çarçoveya têkoşîna li dijî terorê de ti sûcekî nîşan nadin û bal kişand ser ku bersûc xwendekarên zanîngehê ne.


Dadgehê biryara tehliyeya Duruyê da. Darizandina Duruyê dê bê girtin berdewam bike.


Danişîn taloqî 7ê Kanûna Paşîna 2027an kirin.

author: Isaac Nellist, Chiara Reeves
title: USyd students vote to cut ties with Israel
content:
Students at the University of Sydney (USyd) have overwhelmingly voted for an academic boycott of Israel in a referendum held alongside elections for the Student Representative Council (SRC) over September 22–24.

Honi Soit reported that more than 3500 students, 86% of the 4065 students who voted, were in favour of calling on USyd to adopt an “academic boycott policy against Israeli institutions complicit in apartheid and genocide”.

The referendum motion called on the university to cut ties with Israeli universities, including Tel Aviv University, Technion and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

It also called on management to “end all research partnerships with weapons companies supplying Israel” and for the SRC to “support the struggle for Palestinian freedom”.

All four candidates for SRC President supported the referendum, including incumbent president Grace Street from Grassroots, Emma Searle from Socialist Alternative (SAlt), Ava Cavalerie from National Labor Students (NLS) and Vieve Carnsew from Solidarity.

The referendum was activated by Carnsew and Students Against War/Solidarity after they collected at least 500 signatures.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese gave Carnsew and Solidarity’s “Globalise the Intifada” ticket more coverage by describing it as a “hateful slogan”.

Albanese, NSW Premier Chris Minns and federal Education Minister Jason Clare reportedly contacted university management about the campaign. USyd Vice-Chancellor Mark Scott described the ticket a “psycho social hazard” and banned the ticket from using its signage on parts of the campus.

The Globalise the Intifada ticket said “the smears against our slogan are racist attempts to cover for these crimes that our government and university are complicit in”. “Intifada is the Arabic word for uprising … we are proud to campaign under the slogan. It is a call to end the genocide in Gaza and to free Palestine.”

The referendum result indicates that students support the university taking stronger action to support Palestine and oppose Israel’s genocide.

“Management is attacking the ticket whose members initiated the referendum … this is another blatant attack on the Palestine movement on campus, and an attack on free speech,” Students Against War said on social media.

Honi Soit’s exit polls say Street is likely to win an unprecedented second term as SRC President, collecting 41% of the primary vote. This was followed by Cavalerie (30.5%), Searle (20%) and Carnsew (2.88%).

SAlt won the highest percentage of SRC council votes, with 25%. This was followed by Grassroots (22%), NLS (13%) and PENTA (13%).

Street told Honi Soit that: “Students have said ‘Enough is enough’, that they stand against these oppressive systems and institutions, and that they are fed up with our university’s complicity in apartheid and genocide. We need collective action and a strong student movement, and that’s exactly what students have voted for.”

[Isaac Nellist and Chiara Reeves are students at the University of Sydney. Reeves stood on the Grassroots for Queer Liberation ticket.]

author: Laura Hernández
title: Clinton-Era Laws Passed 30 Years Ago Enabled Trump’s Anti-Immigrant Agenda.
content:
Clinton’s ‘96 laws provided the legal foundation for mass detention, rapid deportations, and the evasion of due process.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The more the American public sees of President Donald Trump’s hardline, anti-immigrant policies in action — the deaths, military-style invasions of neighborhoods, and mass detention and deportations — the more his approval on the issue drops.

If this trend sounds familiar, it’s because a similar wave of disapproval played out in Trump’s first term. Despite that backlash, Trump returned to office embracing even more extreme measures.

We must finally confront and uproot the core of the U.S.’s anti-immigrant underbelly, which is largely reflected in the racially motivated notion of criminalization.

Trump was not the first politician to exploit the concept of criminality, and he certainly won’t be the last. Criminalizing narratives are deeply planted in the American psyche, and they have commonly acted as the vessel through which white supremacist rhetoric and policy are ingrained into our culture and laws.

In the late 1980’s, criminalization went mainstream in the form of racist dog whistles, particularly those hinging on vile anti-Blackness deployed by politicians seeking to activate white voters. In the decades since, conservative and liberal leaders alike more purposefully extended this criminality framework to immigration — so much so that it’s now perhaps the primary driver of the public immigration debate.

Consider how Americans of all political stripes are often presented with the binary choice of supporting the “right” type of immigrant. In this oversimplification, immigrants fall into categories like “good” or “bad,” “legal” or “illegal,” “deserving” or “undeserving.”

Trump did not invent these narratives. They’ve underpinned both major parties’ politics of immigration for several decades, despite their basis in fiction and fear-mongering rather than evidence and compassion, or the fact these narratives are weaponized against non-white immigrants who for centuries have disproportionately faced restrictive and punitive policies for the act of seeking relief in this country.

But Trump’s partisan opposition, despite its massive opportunities in the face of unpopular, hardline policies, has repeatedly failed to capture the public’s long-term support on immigration. Too often, Democrats repackage the same old criminalizing narratives — often in softer terms, but always in line with the oversimplified good-or-bad thinking. This lack of imagination is reflected in the nearly annual bipartisan votes to increase funding for federal enforcement agencies like Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, as well as Democratic leaders’ messaging and policies.

Take, for example, former President Barack Obama’s push to deport “felons, not families”; Joe Biden squandering his mandate to reverse the cruelty of Trump’s first term by continuing many Trump policies, like Title 42 and the backing of for-profit immigrant detention; or Kamala Harris, in her presidential bid, focusing much of her immigration rhetoric on “securing” the border.

It’s a toxic cycle: The public rightfully disapproves of the atrocities of anti-immigrant policies; in response, liberals roll out unimaginative plans hinged on outdated narratives; and finally, in the vacuum created by the lack of any tangible, pro-immigrant vision, the right recaptures the public’s attention with fear mongering and a sensationalist focus on crime and the border.

To break this cycle, we must imagine a pro-immigrant future in which our communities, not politicians and pundits, get to define safety.

We can start with recognizing that the modern-day legal basis for the criminalization of immigrants largely rests on a pair of anti-immigrant bills signed into law by Bill Clinton 30 years ago. Building upon the U.S. legacy of racialized immigration control, the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA) and the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA) further entrenched mass incarceration and laid the blueprint for the detention and deportation machine we have today.

These laws drastically expanded the government’s ability to automatically detain and deport people without due process and without consideration for their current circumstances.

author: Clare Hymer
title: Who Does the Green Party’s ‘Zionism Is Racism’ Motion Really Serve?
content:
It’s Saturday morning in a Victorian public garden in Camden, north London, and the mood is upbeat. Green leader Zack Polanski is fighting a byelection in suboptimal conditions: in a seat with an 11,000 Labour majority, his approval ratings in a slump, and, unlike when the party won Gorton and Denton in February, a prime minister in Downing Street who not everyone totally hates. But on his side he has a party membership surpassing 230,000, of whom around 200 enthusiastic volunteers are out today. If Green members are apparently

“turning on” Polanski for not being anti-Zionist enough

, as one recent report in the rightwing press claimed, you can’t feel it here. 


But that’s not to say Zionism isn’t being talked about. It is, as much on this sunny morning in Holborn and St Pancras as in the media in recent weeks, because of a controversial motion titled ‘Zionism is Racism’, set to be debated at the party’s conference just days before the 8 October byelection.


The Greens already have strong policies on Israel and Palestine, describing Israeli conduct as apartheid and genocide, backing a full arms embargo, sanctions and an end to occupation and illegal settlements. But the Zionism is Racism motion takes things further. It calls on the party to, among other things, state that it is anti-Zionist, support a single, democratic Palestinian state, demand freedom for Palestinian political prisoners, oppose the Palestine Action ban, affirm Palestinians’ right to resistance, and, as per the title, equate Zionism with racism.


The motion itself isn’t new, and nor is the hoo-ha around it. Submitted to the party’s spring conference but not put to members due to time constraints (

or sabotage

, depending on who you ask), it was leapt on by the rightwing press as evidence of a Green antisemitism crisis. By avoiding debating the motion back in March, the party just kicked the can down the road, Novara Media reporter

Rivkah Brown wrote at the time

. But some think that a fight, both with the media and within the party, is exactly what’s needed.


“The whole point of this motion is for us to challenge and confront the establishment,”

said Lubna Speitan

, a British-Palestinian activist and the proposer of the motion. “It doesn’t matter what the leadership thinks… It’s about us, the members… forcing their hand.”


Speitan’s comments followed

an interview

 in which Polanski, who’s been under pressure to take a stance, said he was undecided about voting for the motion. He did say he believed it needed to better safeguard anti-Zionist Jews from being accused of racism, and it should be up to the people of the region to determine their own political settlement, not the Green party of England and Wales or the British state. Still, on Thursday night, Polanski sat in front of the Board of Deputies of British Jews and declared he was an anti-Zionist – something supporters of the motion

claimed as a win

.


Ashok Kumar, a Green member who’s backing the motion, told Novara Media: “It’s the right position”.


“[The] politics of the country have shifted quite dramatically since late 2023,” Kumar said. “We’re actually meeting the proportion of the population that really feels strongly about this.


“There is no fence-sitting on this… Some things aren’t nuanced. Slavery, not nuanced. Zionism, not nuanced… The point is to throw down the gauntlet and say, ‘You’re either with the people of Palestine, or you’re with the oppressors’.” 


But even anti-Zionist members who don’t find much to disagree with in the content of the motion have raised doubts about whether or not it’s strategic. Some activists are dismissive of the media ire it’s drawing: “Come at us,” said Kumar, “You stand up to the press… and people actually respect that.” But others believe a big debate about Zionism could harm the party’s electoral chances – and without doing anything to make Palestinians’ lives any better. 


“It’s quite an abstract debate, it’s quite an academic debate”, said a local party chair, who asked to remain anonymous due to his role. “It’s not particularly relevant for most people in the country at large.”


A Green councillor in south London agreed. “[The motion] traps us at the level of language and definitions… There’s a perception that there’s a dial called ‘anti-Zionism’ and the higher you turn it, the more Palestinian liberation you get. And obviously that’s not true.”


This isn’t an argument for not talking about Palestine. Joe Todd, a writer …

author: Ishita Chakrabarty
title: Hindus for Human Rights: ‘Racism is not just about violence, it manifests through misinformation’
content:
To all those who have come from far off-lands and continents; who have made it here despite the monumental barriers that passport privilege poses for some over others — the intense questioning as to motivation; the demand for return tickets; the visa costs that keep escalating year on year; the bank statements and medical reports to prove you will not become a burden onto the system, I am one among you.

To those who have lived here for generations and are yet still told to “Go back where you came from”.

To those who hold a sacred relationship to this land — whose belonging to this land can never be severed by the operation of an unjust, extractive and foreign imposed law.

And to all those who join us here in solidarity, who believe in the idea of an inclusive, egalitarian and multicultural Australia.

I come from Bengal in India. I am representing Hindus for Human Rights, a voice for progressive Hindus and Indians working for inter-faith and inter-community respect and understanding and advocating against all kinds of discrimination and bigotry.

Coming from India, I know all too well what hate, bigotry and the belief of the superiority of some over the other looks like, and how the destruction of the very fabric of society is tantamount to the destruction of the human within us.

It is because of the love I hold towards my home country and the appreciation for being here that I believe we must join hands in the fight against racism and bigotry, whether it comes from the far right politics of One Nation, or from the Hindutva ideology that considers Dalits, Muslims, Christians and other minorities inferior and less than human.

As I speak, Muslims are being lynched, evicted, legally stripped of their citizenship through complicit state institutions. Christians are being hounded, their prayer services are being stopped mid-worship on allegations of forced conversions. Dalits and other caste minorities remain trapped in a system where the so-called upper castes get offended by someone for sporting a moustache, or a Dalit man “daring” to attend their own wedding on horseback.

As a person bearing a majoritarian identity, I feel even more compelled to not only speak of racism emanating from a certain and distant political entity, but also the hatred, transpiring within our own South Asian community, including in Australia.

Identities, beliefs and practices travel alongside communities and are often seen through acts such as questioning one’s food preferences, tasking that one Indian student whose identity is given away by their surname to undertake the menial tasks in the house, through casual bullying. They perpetrate through closed social groups and in marriage alliances.

Hindus for Human Rights along with allies have worked hard and successfully to have caste discrimination included as a form of racism in city councils and universities.

When we speak of racism and bigotry it is also important to speak about these internal exclusions that we have created. For the same hatred that I mentioned earlier is then taken and twisted to justify that the far right is not against all immigrants — only the “bad ones” who refuse to “assimilate”, for example, the hijab- or turban-wearing student of Indian origin.

It is used to legitimise the exclusion of our fellow community members, as when One Nation leader Pauline Hanson keeps speaking of how Indians are the “good, hardworking migrants”.

It is seen when platforms show her attending Diwali festivals and being warmly received by diasporic Indians, represented through associations like the Hindu Council of Australia, or when she visits that one Indian migrant-run shop in Townsville, posing with the owner while eating fish and chips.

When I speak of racism, I speak of the overt acts: The people who called 22-year-old Harmanpreet Singh “a dog”, and physically assaulted him, leaving him with a broken nose in February in Corio. Or when they called 26-year-old Nayonika a “curry muncher”, “smelly Indian”, and a “Mrs. 7/11 driver” in Sydney’s CBD.

But racism also manifests through misinformation such as caricatures portraying Indians, and other immigrants, as being responsible for the housing crisis.

It co-exists in the digital world where desk warriors feel confident to call Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi “a filthy Australian hating racist pig”.

It does not stop at that. Racism and bigotry also acts through constant daily acts of micro-aggression; through people staring you …

author: Frenny Jowi
title: Congo in Kenya: Why Xenophobia is a Racist Ideal
content:
Thirty-three-year-old Emmanuel is a freelance hairdresser in Nairobi. He is a refugee from the Democratic Republic of Congo and has lived in Kenya for six years.


The young man is chic, dressed in designer brands, with a gentle demeanour that reflects his customer-care style in the city’s beauty industry. His calm, collected appearance belies a history of strife, struggle, and an ongoing effort to recover from the decades of armed conflict he witnessed as a child in North Kivu.


‘I will never forget the night when rebels attacked our village in North Kivu. I must have been seven years old at that time. Some people were killed, and there was fire burning everywhere around us.’


Emmanuel narrated his story as he swung around in his styling chair in front of a large mirror that is popularly called a ‘station’ in Nairobi’s hairdressing and beauty salons.


I had visited Emmanuel at the salon where he works. Renting business premises in Nairobi is a significant cost for many young business owners, whether citizen or foreigner. In the beauty industry, most professionals can only afford to rent a mirror and a styling chair as a workstation – hence the name ‘station’.


While occasionally glancing at his WhatsApp notifications for customer bookings, Emmanuel continued to share his story with me.


‘The attack happened many years ago. I still remember how my mother stopped to pack her pot of fish stew and cassava leaves and rice. My father asked her to hurry up, leave the food, and run for safety, but she insisted she would not leave her delicious food. As we all escaped in the dim light of the moon, I recall our neighbours’ comments about my mother’s weird sense of what to salvage. She insisted the food would also save us and she would not leave it behind despite the gunfire. Now I find that funny.’


Emmanuel laughed, trying to find humour in a devastating story.


I knew that talking about traumatic childhood experiences from war would be difficult, so I did not press Emmanuel further about the night armed fighters attacked their village, killing many people and setting houses on fire.


The events Emmanuel witnessed as a child in 2000 were part of the Second Congo War, dubbed Africa’s World War. According to

Amnesty International

, the DRC’s current conflict has been ongoing since the 1990s, particularly in the eastern part of the country, which borders South Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and Tanzania.


This armed conflict escalated in August 1998 when President Laurent Kabila fell out with the Ugandan and Rwandan allies who had helped him seize power.


Emmanuel narrated how the fighting between the Lendu-Ngiti and the opposing Hema began as communal land disputes involving farmers and pastoralists. Locals believe politicians and those with mining interests took advantage of these seemingly solvable disputes to fuel the ongoing war. He added that their radio broadcasts often mentioned various fighting groups such as the UPDF (Uganda People’s Defence Forces) and the UPC (United Congolese Patriots).


‘In the news, when we heard that Bosco Ntaganda was in court and wanted to defend himself in Kinyarwanda, we were all shocked, because locally, we knew him as one of us. We never thought he was from Rwanda. He lived here for so long, spoke our language, looked like one of us, and was always involved in Congolese affairs,’ Emmanuel said.


Decades of conflict have been fuelled by ethnic tensions, political rivalries, corruption, and fighting for control of valuable natural resources.


Over time, the war drew in nine African nations, making it one of the largest wars in African history. The 2017 Kivu Security Tracker Report by Jason Stearns and Christoph Vogel listed 132 armed fighter groups operating in North and South Kivu alone.


Today, Emmanuel is one of the over 100 million citizens of the DRC affected by incessant wars. The DRC is the fourth most populous country in Africa and the 14th in the world. Despite decades of war and pandemics such as Ebola, its population has continued to grow steadily. 


In 2025,

Human Rights Watch

 reported that the Congolese military and a coalition of armed fighters have continued to attack civilians. The report adds that throughout 2024, the

Rwandan

 army and the M23 armed group indiscriminately shelled displacement camps and other densely populated areas near Goma in eastern Congo.


Emmanuel arrived in Kenya in 2019, just before the COVID-19 pandemic. Earlier, in 2017 …

title: Tormenta Negra 2: “no son políticas de prevención del delito, es racismo”
content:
El gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires realizó el jueves 24 un nuevo operativo “Tormenta Negra” en 15 barrios populares con violencia policial, detenciones arbitrarias y el retiro de pertenencias y herramientas de trabajo. Jorge Macri “consolida una política que identifica pobreza con inseguridad” e insiste en violentar la vida en los barrios populares y atemorizar a quienes viven en ellos, denunciaron desde el Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS). “No existen operativos de este tipo en los otros barrios de la Ciudad” como Palermo, Caballito o Núñez, señalaron.


Compartimos el comunicado del CELS:


Tormenta Negra 2: el gobierno de CABA entiende a los barrios populares como zonas de ocupación


El gobierno de Jorge Macri volvió a desplegar más de 1500 policías y agentes de control en 15 villas y barrios populares de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires. Registramos episodios de violencia policial, detenciones arbitrarias y el retiro de pertenencias y herramientas de trabajo. La CABA consolida una política que identifica pobreza con inseguridad, no con ausencia de derechos.


El jueves 24 de septiembre, el gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires realizó un nuevo operativo Tormenta Negra en 15 villas y barrios populares. Más de 1500 policías y agentes de control de Espacio Público ingresaron de manera simultánea a los barrios para realizar controles de personas y vehículos, inspeccionar comercios y retirar del espacio público objetos de las personas que viven allí. Es la segunda vez que el gobierno porteño organiza un despliegue de estas características, después del de mayo de este año. Jorge Macri insiste en violentar la vida en los barrios populares y atemorizar a quienes viven en ellos.


Se trata de un modo de entender la ciudad y el derecho a la ciudad con un abordaje racializante y con límites de clase. Es una política que decide qué cuerpos van a ser controlados por la policía, qué familias van a ser desalojadas sin garantías, qué personas deberán demostrar una y otra vez que tienen derecho a quedarse y cuáles tienen que mostrar su documentación en las estaciones de trenes y subtes. La política porteña naturaliza que la principal y primera intervención del Estado en los barrios populares va a ser la policial. Uno de los jóvenes detenidos estaba en situación de calle dentro de la Villa 21. El gobierno llegó con patrulleros, efectivos armados y agentes de control, en lugar de organizar una intervención a partir de las necesidades de quienes viven allí o para garantizar los derechos sobre los que el mismo Estado está en deuda. No hubo presencia de áreas de desarrollo social, sino el despliegue de dispositivos de estigmatización de quienes viven allí, para convertirlos en sujetos de sospecha. El gobierno de la Ciudad abandonó las políticas de integración sociourbana. Ahora se enfoca en una política que niega la ciudadanía de las personas que viven en estos barrios. No existen operativos de este tipo en los otros barrios de la Ciudad, que los invadan a la pesca de ver qué delitos se identifican, que sin duda los hay en Palermo, Caballito o Núñez.


La vara en la Ciudad de Buenos Aires está tan baja que tenemos que reiterar lo obvio: en los barrios populares viven personas que trabajan, estudian, crían a sus hijos que van a la escuela y sostienen redes comunitarias. Tienen derecho a tener políticas que integren las villas con la ciudad en términos de derechos garantizados: a la vivienda, a la salud, a la educación, al trabajo y no estar sujeto a control poblacional permanente. La guerra contra los pobres habla de la pobreza en políticas públicas de la gestión actual de la ciudad. Y del solapamiento de un abordaje que se anuncia como control de actividades delictivas con la persecución de las estrategias de supervivencia. De este modo, la ciudad se fragmenta cada vez más. Los operativos espasmódicos y violentos no llevan orden a estos barrios, sino incertidumbre, abusos y show para las redes sociales. Cuando terminan los operativos y la policía se retira de estos barrios, no permanecen otras políticas públicas.


Durante el operativo del jueves registramos situaciones de violencia policial, uso de gases lacrimógenos y disparos de balas de goma. En la Villa 21-24, los registros audiovisuales que hicieron los mismos vecinos muestran intervenciones contra personas en situación de calle que intentaban resguardar sus colchones y pertenencias. feministesrevolutionnaires.org


Pour qu'il n'y ait plus aucune violence


Depuis l'irruption de #MeToo en 2017, la question des violences sexistes et sexuelles s'est inscrite durablement parmi les préoccupations majeures de la population. Chaque année, le décompte des féminicides fait la une des journaux. Les dénonciations de violences mettant en cause des figures publiques sont largement médiatisées. Les affaires suscitant l'émotion populaire se succèdent.


En parallèle, on observe un développement rapide des mobilisations féministes, avec des marches massives aux dates emblématiques du 8 mars (journée internationale pour les droits des femmes) et du 25 novembre (journée internationale contre les violences de genre). Bien que ses détracteurs restent très audibles, le mouvement féministe gagne en force et en audience et ses idées et ses discours se diffusent amplement.


Malgré ces éléments favorables,

le mouvement féministe peine à faire émerger des revendications concrètes

 capables d'enrayer à grande échelle les violences sexistes et sexuelles. Pourtant, on ne manque pas de ressources pour comprendre les mécanismes qui permettent les violences. Comment expliquer, alors, que nous ayons tant de mal à y répondre

 

?


Il faut dire que

la tâche est d'une ampleur colossale

 : on estime que près de 280 000 femmes et 160 000 enfants sont victimes de violences chaque année. Et le mouvement féministe se fixe comme objectif, ambitieux, de

réduire ces chiffres à zéro

 

! Or les violences sexistes et sexuelles, au-delà des rapports de pouvoir individuels entre un agresseur et sa victime, contribuent à maintenir l'exploitation des femmes. Par la peur, ces violences disciplinent les femmes et les contraignent à des rôles bien précis dans le système capitaliste : effectuer gratuitement les tâches domestiques au sein de leur foyer, subir des emplois sous-payés dans les secteurs les plus dévalorisés du marché du travail (soin, éducation, entretien…). Pour nous, réduire à zéro les violences sexistes et sexuelles, cela nécessite donc de

transformer radicalement la société en détruisant tout le système patriarcal, raciste et capitaliste : de faire la révolution

.


D'ici là, une série d'étapes intermédiaires peuvent faire baisser les violences. Nous avons tenté de les regrouper dans ce


Programme d'urgence féministe en 13 mesures


. En partant d'une analyse sur les causes des violences, nous déterminons quels leviers il faudrait actionner en priorité pour les faire reculer, et, de là, quelles mesures revendiquer.


La précarité : un accélérateur des violences


Si les violences sexistes et sexuelles existent dans toutes les couches de la société, elles ne touchent pas tout le monde de la même manière. On dit souvent que le viol et l'inceste n'ont ni classe sociale, ni couleur de peau, ni religion. Mais en ce qui concerne les violences conjugales et, dans leur forme la plus extrême, le féminicide, certaines conditions sociales augmentent le risque d'y être exposée.


Les données disponibles suggèrent que

la précarité

,

la dépendance économique

 vis-à-vis d'un conjoint et les inégalités de revenus au sein des couples sont des facteurs qui augmentent significativement le risque d'être victime de violences. Ainsi, dans plus de 80% des cas de féminicides conjugaux en France, les victimes sont soit sans emploi ou retraitées, soit ouvrières ou employées

 [

1

]

]. Les cadres et professions intellectuelles supérieures sont, à l'inverse, très peu représentées. Il existe aussi des corrélations entre les pertes d'emploi, les baisses de revenus et l'augmentation des violences dans les foyers

 [

2

]

].


La conclusion est simple :

la dépendance économique à un conjoint violent est un véritable obstacle à la séparation

, d'autant plus avec des enfants à charge et des aides sociales insuffisantes. Par ailleurs, le motif de la séparation non acceptée est le deuxième mobile invoqué par les hommes qui tuent leur compagne.


La précarité n'est pas qu'une question de catégorie …

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: A Failed Reception System in Crete Turns People on the Move Into Political Targets
content:
Athanatoi, Greece — Residents of a small village in Northern Crete, near Herakleion, are fighting the Greek government’s plan to convert a disused factory into a reception center for people on the move, escalating a monthslong standoff that pits xenophobic backlash against an increasingly securitized European border regime. 


“We’re not staying silent. We’re not backing down. No to the camp.” The slogan, painted in red and black across a large banner, hangs from the gate of a factory facing the Candia-Mires state highway, near the village of Athanatoi in northern Crete. A few yards away, a second banner reads: “No camp — the people have a voice.”


A banner reading “We’re not staying silent. We’re not backing down. No to the camp,” hanging from the gate of a factory opposite the abandoned Skouloudis industrial complex. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Across the road stands the disused Skouloudis industrial complex, recently identified by Greece’s Ministry of Migration and Asylum as a site to be converted into a reception center for migrants crossing the stretch of sea between Libya and Greece and landing on the island’s southern coast. Since Minister Thanos Plevris

announced

 the plan in mid-June 2026, Skouloudis has been at the center of a

bitter standoff

 between authorities and local communities.


The former Skouloudis industrial facility, seen from the Heraklion–Mires state highway. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


The choice of this industrial site, however, is only the latest development in a long and contested decision-making process that began in the summer of 2025, when

arrivals in Crete

 far outpaced those recorded along the Aegean route — the sea passage from Turkey to the Greek islands of Lesbos, Samos and Chios that has long been the country’s primary migration corridor — making the island Greece’s main point of entry.


Against a backdrop of chronic absence of adequate first-reception facilities on the island, the handling of landings has fallen to entirely

unsustainable emergency measures

.


The main temporary holding site in Heraklion remains the former psygeio — a Coast Guard cold-storage building in the port area. Meant to hold just 70 to 80 people, the site held more than 450 in the first months of 2026, forcing men, women and children to sleep on the floor.


The lack of adequate sanitation and ventilation created dire health conditions, while pressure to find an alternative mounted further as the Port Authority pursued legal action to clear the site. Faced with this infrastructural collapse, authorities found themselves forced to publicly propose a solution.


One of the rooms inside the temporary first-reception facility known as Psygeio, in the port of Heraklion, where people are held after their arrival. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Locked Up and Criminalized: People on the Move Face a Broken System on Crete’s Shores


Between Delay and Denial 


In the summer of 2025, the government

announced

 the conversion of several military sites, but that announcement was followed by months of silence and effective inaction. Only in February 2026 did the Greek Parliament approve the opening of

two centers

, without specifying their location or how they would be built.


The first details came only months later: in Chania, authorities settled on retrofitting

Agya

, a former exhibition center already in use as a temporary reception facility; in Heraklion, the disused Skouloudis industrial plant was identified instead.


“These delays and constant changes of plan shouldn’t be read as political strategy, but as failure,” Michalis Markodimitrakis, a member of the Heraklion-based collective Thalassa of Solidarity and a researcher at the Hellenic Mediterranean University, told Unicorn Riot.


“Local communities and representatives of Crete’s tourism and cultural sector are pushing back hard, because they see the presence of migrants as damaging to the island’s image and a threat to their economic interests.”


Michalis Markodimitrakis, member of Thalassa of Solidarity collective


A side view of the former Skouloudis industrial facility, where adaptation works to accommodate people on the move have not yet begun. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Back in July 2025, the day after the first announcement floated the opening of the centers, a network of tourism industry associations sent an

open letter

 to Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Migration and …
